Except for the [Back Bay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Back_Bay,_Boston "Back Bay, Boston") and part of the South Boston neighborhoods, Boston has no [street grid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Street_grid "Street grid"). The City of Boston, composed of many smaller towns annexed over the years, retained most of the pre-existing street names, resulting in many duplicates throughout the city.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

Expressways and freeways in and around Greater Boston are laid out with two circumferential expressways: [Interstate 495](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interstate_495_in_Massachusetts "Interstate 495 in Massachusetts") and [Route 128](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massachusetts_Route_128 "Massachusetts Route 128"). The circumferential routes are intersected by several radial highways, including:

*   [Interstate 93](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interstate_93 "Interstate 93") (the Northern/Southeast Expressway), which extends north of the city into [New Hampshire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Hampshire "New Hampshire"), and southward to the [Braintree Split](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Braintree_Split "Braintree Split"),
*   [Interstate 90](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interstate_90 "Interstate 90") (the Massachusetts Turnpike), connecting Boston with [Worcester](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Worcester,_Massachusetts "Worcester, Massachusetts") and [Springfield](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Springfield,_Massachusetts "Springfield, Massachusetts"),
*   [United States Route 1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Route_1 "United States Route 1") (the Northeast Expressway/Newburyport Turnpike), crossing the [Tobin Bridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tobin_Bridge "Tobin Bridge") and eventually serving [Newburyport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newburyport,_Massachusetts "Newburyport, Massachusetts"),
*   [Storrow Drive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Storrow_Drive "Storrow Drive"), an unnumbered high-speed parkway along the [Charles River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_River "Charles River") connecting downtown Boston with the Route 2 corridor,
*   [U.S. Route 20](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Route_20 "U.S. Route 20"), a route running from Kenmore Square to Newport, Oregon — although it is not an expressway.
*   [Massachusetts Route 2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massachusetts_Route_2 "Massachusetts Route 2") (the Concord Turnpike/Alewife Brook Parkway), serving the northwestern suburbs including [Lexington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lexington,_Massachusetts "Lexington, Massachusetts"), [Concord](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Concord,_Massachusetts "Concord, Massachusetts") and [Fitchburg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fitchburg,_Massachusetts "Fitchburg, Massachusetts"),
*   [Massachusetts Route 3](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massachusetts_Route_3 "Massachusetts Route 3") (the Pilgrims Highway), connecting Boston with [Cape Cod](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cape_Cod "Cape Cod"),
*   [United States Route 3](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Route_3 "United States Route 3") (the Northwest Expressway), a functionally separate highway serving [Lowell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lowell,_Massachusetts "Lowell, Massachusetts"), [Burlington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burlington,_Massachusetts "Burlington, Massachusetts") and other suburbs in between Route 2 and I-93,
*   [Massachusetts Route 24](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massachusetts_Route_24 "Massachusetts Route 24"), serving the interior southern suburbs, including [Brockton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brockton,_Massachusetts "Brockton, Massachusetts"), [Taunton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taunton,_Massachusetts "Taunton, Massachusetts") and [Fall River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River,_Massachusetts "Fall River, Massachusetts")
*   and [Interstate 95](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interstate_95 "Interstate 95"), indirectly connecting Boston with [Rhode Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhode_Island "Rhode Island") via I-93.

By the early 1990s, traffic on the elevated downtown portions of I-93 and Route 1 (the Central Artery) was 190,000 vehicles per day, with an accident rate four times the national average for urban interstates. Traffic was bumper-to-bumper for six to eight hours per day, with projections of traffic jams doubling by 2010. Also, the elevated structure itself was decaying, after more than a half century of continuous use. For most of the 1990s and early 2000s, driving in Boston was disrupted by the [Big Dig](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_Dig "Big Dig"), the most expensive (roughly $14 billion) road project in the history of the US.

After more than 15 years of disruption, The Big Dig, along with other highway projects, provided less than 10 years of relief before congestion returned to the levels seen in "prerecession 2005, when the Big Dig was almost complete and marketed as the solution to gridlock for commuters ... analyses would conclude that the added capacity attracted more drivers, and pushed the traffic bottlenecks farther into the suburbs."[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transportation_in_Boston#cite_note-1) However even without the big dig the raised road was structurally deficient and needed rebuilding or replacement.

Boston remains one of the most congested metropolitan areas in the US. The complex and still-changing road network, with many one-way streets and time-based traffic restrictions, has led many Boston travelers to consider an up-to-date [GPS navigation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GPS_navigation "GPS navigation") map system a necessity.

### Walking and bicycling

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Transportation_in_Boston&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Walking and bicycling")]

[![Image 8: Major US City Commute Patterns 2021](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/53/USCommutePatternsTimeCommute.png/500px-USCommutePatternsTimeCommute.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:USCommutePatternsTimeCommute.png)

Compared to residents of other American cities, Bostonians have average commute times and high rates of public transit use.

[![Image 9: Historical Commute Patterns in Boston 2006–2021](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/61/Boston_Historical_Commute_Patterns.png/500px-Boston_Historical_Commute_Patterns.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Boston_Historical_Commute_Patterns.png)

Bostonians shifted to driving alone, at the expense of public transit as a result of the [COVID-19 pandemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic "COVID-19 pandemic"), but continued to walk at the highest rates of any US major city.

Boston is known to travel agents as "America's Walking City", has been rated as the third most [walkable](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walkability "Walkability") city in the US by [Walk Score](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walk_Score "Walk Score"), and also has a high Transit Score.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transportation_in_Boston#cite_note-WalkScore-2)

Boston is a compact city, sized right for walking or bicycling. According to a _[Prevention](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prevention\_(magazine) "Prevention (magazine)")_ magazine report in 2003, the city has the highest percentage of on-foot commuters of any city in the United States. In 2000, 13.36% of Boston commuters [walked to work](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_U.S._cities_with_most_pedestrian_commuters "List of U.S. cities with most pedestrian commuters") according to the [US Census](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Census "United States Census"). This was the highest of any major US city, bested only by college towns such as nearby [Cambridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cambridge,_Massachusetts "Cambridge, Massachusetts"). Most of the area's cities and towns have standing committees devoted to improvements to the bicycle and pedestrian environment. The first pedestrian advocacy organization in the United States, WalkBoston, was started in Boston in 1990, and helped start the national pedestrian advocacy organization America Walks.

Cycling is popular in Boston, for both recreation and commuting. Some bicycle paths are marked on some roadways, but very few completely separated paths are available to cyclists. The [Minuteman Bikeway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minuteman_Bikeway "Minuteman Bikeway") (which runs through several suburbs northwest of Boston) and the [Charles River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_River "Charles River") bike paths are popular with recreational cyclists and tourists. The [Emerald Necklace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emerald_Necklace "Emerald Necklace") system of parklands and parkways, pioneered by [Frederick Law Olmsted](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Law_Olmsted "Frederick Law Olmsted") and his sons, provides some more pleasant alternative routes for cyclists. The [Southwest Corridor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southwest_Corridor_(Boston) "Southwest Corridor (Boston)") also provides [cycling infrastructure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cycling_infrastructure "Cycling infrastructure"),[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transportation_in_Boston#cite_note-3) as does the [East Boston Greenway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Boston_Greenway "East Boston Greenway").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transportation_in_Boston#cite_note-4) Many MBTA riders use a bicycle to get to a nearby station, and the number of bicycle racks and lockers has been increased.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transportation_in_Boston#cite_note-5)

However [_Bicycling_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bicycling_(magazine) "Bicycling (magazine)") magazine, in its March 2006 issue, named the city as one of its three worst cities in the United States for cycling.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transportation_in_Boston#cite_note-6) The distinction was earned for "lousy roads, scarce and unconnected bike lanes and bike-friendly gestures from City Hall that go nowhere—such as hiring a bike coordinator in 2001, only to cut the position two years later".[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transportation_in_Boston#cite_note-7) Neighboring [Cambridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cambridge,_Massachusetts "Cambridge, Massachusetts") earned an honorable mention as one of the best cities for cycling with a population of 75,000-200,000.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transportation_in_Boston#cite_note-8)

Since September 2007, when Mayor [Thomas Menino](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Menino "Thomas Menino") started a bicycle program called Boston Bikes with a goal of improving bicycling conditions by adding bike lanes and racks and offering bikeshare programs, the city has improved accommodations for bicyclists in a number of ways.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transportation_in_Boston#cite_note-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transportation_in_Boston#cite_note-10) The least visible improvement is zoning and building code changes to encourage showering and locker facilities in major office buildings. Better signage and lane markings for bicyclists are starting to appear. More visible enforcement of traffic regulations on motorists, bicyclists, and pedestrians has commenced.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transportation_in_Boston#cite_note-11)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transportation_in_Boston#cite_note-12)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transportation_in_Boston#cite_note-13)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transportation_in_Boston#cite_note-14)

Boston has an active [Critical Mass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Critical_Mass_(cycling) "Critical Mass (cycling)") ride group, and [MassBike](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MassBike?action=edit&redlink=1 "MassBike (page does not exist)") is a bike advocacy group active in supporting cyclists in the area.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transportation_in_Boston#cite_note-bimag-15)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transportation_in_Boston#cite_note-massbike-16) The [LivableStreets Alliance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LivableStreets_Alliance?action=edit&redlink=1 "LivableStreets Alliance (page does not exist)"), headquartered in Cambridge, is an advocacy group for bicyclists, pedestrians, and walkable neighborhoods.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transportation_in_Boston#cite_note-LSA-17)

#### Maps and guides

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Transportation_in_Boston&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Maps and guides")]

[![Image 10: Horse-drawn carriage at dusk on a city street](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/ca/Bostonhorseandcart.JPG/250px-Bostonhorseandcart.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Bostonhorseandcart.JPG)

One of several horse carriages transporting tourists around the city

The Boston regional [Metropolitan Area Planning Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metropolitan_Area_Planning_Council "Metropolitan Area Planning Council") (MAPC) publishes a large and detailed "Greater Boston Cycling & Walking Map", which it distributes free of charge.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transportation_in_Boston#cite_note-MAPCBikeMap-18) The map is also available online and in downloadable form, and revisions are solicited from the general public.

In addition, a small private company called Rubel BikeMaps has for many years published and distributed an extensive lineup of books and maps covering Boston, the state of Massachusetts, and nearby areas of New England.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transportation_in_Boston#cite_note-19) These publications are for sale at many bicycle shops, and online. Because of recent expansion of bike lanes and other facilities, plus increased input from the public, it is important to use the most recent editions of these maps and guides.

Rubel BikeMaps also publishes _Car-Free in Boston:a Guide for Locals and Visitors_, still in its 10th edition as of 2015[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Transportation_in_Boston&action=edit).[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transportation_in_Boston#cite_note-CFIB-20) Prepared by the [Association for Public Transportation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Association_for_Public_Transportation "Association for Public Transportation") (APT), this book contains extensive information useful to bicyclists and pedestrians alike, including coverage of intermodal travel and handicapped accessibility. Although the general overview and travel tips are largely still relevant, this classic book has not been updated since 2003, and must be supplemented by current online information.

With widespread use of smartphones and tablet computers, [online mapping](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Online_mapping "Online mapping") services such as [Google Maps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Google_Maps "Google Maps") have become popular aids for pedestrians, cyclists, and motorists. The MBTA was one of the earliest large transit agencies to embrace the [Open Data](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_Data "Open Data") philosophy, making route, scheduling, and [real-time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real-time_locating_system "Real-time locating system") vehicle location information publicly available in the standard [GTFS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_Transit_Feed_Specification "General Transit Feed Specification") format.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transportation_in_Boston#cite_note-MBTA-GTFS-21) As a result, many third-party apps are available on a number of hardware platforms, allowing riders a wide range of choices in obtaining travel information.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transportation_in_Boston#cite_note-MBTA-Tools-22) Google Maps has started to present maps of the interiors of underground subway stations, and this information is available on Android and iOS smartphones, as well as web browsers.

### Buses

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Transportation_in_Boston&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Buses")]

[![Image 11](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/18/MBTA_route_77_bus_on_Mount_Auburn_Street%2C_October_2019.jpg/250px-MBTA_route_77_bus_on_Mount_Auburn_Street%2C_October_2019.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:MBTA_route_77_bus_on_Mount_Auburn_Street,_October_2019.jpg)

An MBTA bus on Mount Auburn Street in 2019

162 [MBTA bus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MBTA_bus "MBTA bus") routes operate within the Greater Boston area, with a combined ridership of approximately 375,000 one-way trips per day, making it the [seventh-busiest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_United_States_local_bus_agencies_by_ridership "List of United States local bus agencies by ridership") local bus agency in the country. The bus fare is $1.70 with a [CharlieCard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CharlieCard "CharlieCard"), or $2 with a CharlieTicket or cash; monthly commuter passes are available, as are reduced fare transfers between most bus lines and the subway.

In an effort to provide service intermediate in speed and capacity between subways and buses, the MBTA has begun projects using [bus rapid transit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bus_rapid_transit "Bus rapid transit") (BRT) technology. The MBTA has one BRT line, the [Silver Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silver_Line_(MBTA) "Silver Line (MBTA)"), although this operates in two discontinuous sections. The Silver Line operates in part via dedicated trolleybus tunnel, in part via on-street reserved [bus lanes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bus_lane "Bus lane"), and in part mixed with general street traffic. Service through the trolleybus tunnel is by [dual-mode buses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dual-mode_bus "Dual-mode bus"), which operate electrically in the tunnel and within a short section on the surface, and which use diesel power for the rest of the route.

[Massport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massport "Massport") operates the [Logan Express](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Logan_Express "Logan Express"), an express bus service between Logan International Airport and suburban park-and-ride lots.

Several privately owned commuter bus services take passengers between the city and suburbs.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transportation_in_Boston#cite_note-23) Transportation Management Associations[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transportation_in_Boston#cite_note-24) also run public shuttles to specific employment centers, such as the EZ Ride for [Kendall Square](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kendall_Square "Kendall Square");[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transportation_in_Boston#cite_note-25) and the Route 128 Business Council shuttles around Alewife, Needham, and Waltham;[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transportation_in_Boston#cite_note-26)[Partners HealthCare](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partners_HealthCare "Partners HealthCare") runs public shuttles among its locations.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transportation_in_Boston#cite_note-27) The MASCO TMA operates six commuter shuttles for the use of [Longwood Medical Area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Longwood_Medical_Area "Longwood Medical Area") employees and students[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transportation_in_Boston#cite_note-28) run by the MASCO TMA for the [Longwood Medical Area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Longwood_Medical_Area "Longwood Medical Area"). The MASCO M2 shuttle between Harvard Square and the LMA via Massachusetts Avenue is available for public use, though tickets or cash card must be purchased in advance.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transportation_in_Boston#cite_note-29) Many colleges and universities also run private shuttles for students and employees.

In June 2014, the Cambridge-based startup [Bridj](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bridj "Bridj") began running "data driven" bus service in core neighborhoods.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transportation_in_Boston#cite_note-30) It uses a mixture of fixed and dynamic routes and pricing, depending on where and when registered members say they want to go.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transportation_in_Boston#cite_note-31)

### Parking

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Transportation_in_Boston&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Parking")]

Since automobiles did not exist in 1630, when Boston was first settled, parking was not a consideration. The city that sprung up around and away from the original North End neighborhood accommodates cars only awkwardly; parking comes at a premium throughout the city. Off-street parking spaces have sold for more than $160,000 on Beacon Hill.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transportation_in_Boston#cite_note-32) On-street parking is the norm in many sections, and the city created a resident permit parking program to reserve street space for permanent residents in certain neighborhoods. The parking permits are free to Boston residents, however, and the program is overused; permitted spaces remain scarce.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transportation_in_Boston#cite_note-33) Meters citywide are priced at $1.25 per hour, and metered spaces are also often difficult to find.

The number of public parking spaces downtown has been capped since the mid-1970s.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transportation_in_Boston#cite_note-34) The number of parking spaces in East and South Boston, and the hours that they may be used, also is restricted by state regulation. This is part of the state Department of Environmental Protection's plan, approved by the [United States Environmental Protection Agency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Environmental_Protection_Agency "United States Environmental Protection Agency") to address the non-compliance of the region with the mandatory [National Ambient Air Quality Standards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Ambient_Air_Quality_Standards "National Ambient Air Quality Standards") for [ozone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ozone "Ozone").[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transportation_in_Boston#cite_note-35)

The MBTA operates several large [park and ride](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Park_and_ride "Park and ride") facilities on its subway and commuter rail lines, close to major highways, providing access to downtown. While most of these tend to fill up with commuters on weekday mornings, they provide a good place for visitors to leave their cars and see the city without parking hassles on evenings and weekends.

## Rail transportation

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Transportation_in_Boston&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Rail transportation")]

Boston has two discrete rail networks. One of these, the MBTA, widely nicknamed "the T", includes elements of [light rail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Light_rail "Light rail")/[streetcar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Streetcar "Streetcar") operation as well as traditional [subway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rapid_transit "Rapid transit") technology. (The Red, Orange, Blue, and Green Lines have no physical rail interconnections with each other, though they are all operated by the MBTA and exchange passengers in shared stations.) The second network forms the Boston area portion of the [North American rail network](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rail_transportation_in_the_United_States "Rail transportation in the United States"), and provides commuter rail, intercity passenger rail and freight rail services.

Although the two networks are essentially unconnected, they do in some places run alongside each other in the same right of way. Interchange stations allow interchange of passengers, but not trains, between subway and commuter rail services. Parts of the subway network also use former common user rail rights of way.

### Subway network

Boston has the oldest subway system in North America, with the first underground streetcar traffic dating back to 1897. Today the whole subway network is owned and operated by the [Massachusetts Bay Transportation Authority](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massachusetts_Bay_Transportation_Authority "Massachusetts Bay Transportation Authority") (MBTA).

In the early 1960s, the then-newly-formed MBTA hired [Cambridge Seven Associates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cambridge_Seven_Associates "Cambridge Seven Associates") to help develop a new [brand identity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brand_identity "Brand identity"). Cambridge Seven came up with a circled T to represent such concepts as "transit", "transportation" and "tunnel." Today, Bostonians call their rapid transit network "the T", and it is the [fourth busiest in the country](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_United_States_rapid_transit_systems_by_ridership "List of United States rapid transit systems by ridership"), with daily ridership of 273,000 trips on its heavy rail and 90,700 on its light rail.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transportation_in_Boston#cite_note-apta2022q4-36) This compares with the [Washington Metro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_Metro "Washington Metro")'s heavy rail daily ridership of 326,300, the [Chicago 'L'](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_'L' "Chicago 'L'")'s 334,200, and Los Angeles's 76,800, but is overshadowed by [New York City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NYCTA "NYCTA")'s 6.335 million average daily weekday trips.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transportation_in_Boston#cite_note-apta2022q4-36)

The one-way fare is $2.40. Monthly commuter passes, and day and week visitor's passes are also available for purchase.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transportation_in_Boston#cite_note-37) There are four [subway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rapid_transit "Rapid transit") lines in the metropolitan Boston area: the [Red Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_Line_(MBTA) "Red Line (MBTA)"), [Green Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Line_(MBTA) "Green Line (MBTA)"), [Orange Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orange_Line_(MBTA) "Orange Line (MBTA)"), and [Blue Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Line_(MBTA) "Blue Line (MBTA)"). The colors of each line have a symbolic meaning: the Blue Line runs under Boston Harbor; the Red Line used to terminate at [Harvard University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvard_University "Harvard University") (whose school color is [crimson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crimson "Crimson")); the Orange Line used to run along Washington Street, which was once called Orange Street; and the Green Line runs along parts of the [Emerald Necklace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emerald_Necklace "Emerald Necklace") into the leafy suburbs of [Brookline](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookline,_Massachusetts "Brookline, Massachusetts") and [Newton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newton,_Massachusetts "Newton, Massachusetts").[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transportation_in_Boston#cite_note-38)

The Green Line is actually four different lines; it starts as one trunk line but then splits into four different branches, the [B](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Line_B_branch "Green Line B branch") (Boston College), [C](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Line_C_branch "Green Line C branch") (Cleveland Circle), [D](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Line_D_branch "Green Line D branch") (Riverside) and [E](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Line_E_branch "Green Line E branch") (Heath Street) trains. Because the split is only relevant on the outbound direction of travel, one may take any train inbound, but when going outbound one must be careful to board the correct train. The Red Line splits as well, with southbound trains going either to Braintree or Ashmont.

Though most of Boston's [rapid transit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rapid_transit "Rapid transit") network is powered via [third rail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_rail "Third rail"), the outermost portions of the Blue Line, as well as all of the Green Line and [Mattapan Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mattapan_Line "Mattapan Line"), are powered via [overhead lines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Overhead_lines "Overhead lines"). The name "subway" is something of a misnomer; as with other systems, large segments run above ground when far from the city's downtown. Additionally, the Green and Mattapan Lines are technically [light-rail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Light-rail "Light-rail") services, using [LRVs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Light_rail_vehicle "Light rail vehicle") and [streetcars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Streetcars "Streetcars") rather than typical [multiple unit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multiple_unit "Multiple unit") heavy railcar equipment. The Ashmont–Mattapan line uses refurbished classic pre-war "[PCC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PCC_streetcar "PCC streetcar")" trolleys on an exclusive right of way; the Green Line relies on modern high-capacity [LRV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Light_rail "Light rail") cars from Japan and Italy.

Starting around 2011, the MBTA introduced overhead displays at the train platform level which indicate estimated arrival times for the next two trains in each direction. In addition, real-time information about train location (and bus location) is available via an [Open Data](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_Data "Open Data") protocol on the Internet, enabling a large number of third-party smartphone apps and web sites to display expected arrival times throughout the MBTA system. The Green Line relies more on operators than its signal system compared to other lines, especially where trams are driven across or even in automobile lanes on surface rails.

#### Elevated sections

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Transportation_in_Boston&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Elevated sections")]

Despite the first rapid transit segment being built underground, many later parts were built as [elevated railways](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elevated_railway "Elevated railway").[_[dubious](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Accuracy\_dispute#Disputed\_statement "Wikipedia:Accuracy dispute")–[discuss](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Talk:Transportation\_in\_Boston#this\_implies\_a\_major\_separation\_in\_time;\_the\_first\_elevated\_was\_only\_4\_years\_later "Talk:Transportation in Boston")_] A century later, most of these elevated railway sections have been replaced by [cut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cut_(earthmoving) "Cut (earthmoving)") or tunnel routing. The only remaining classic elevated structures are the [Green Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Line_(MBTA) "Green Line (MBTA)")'s [Lechmere Viaduct](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lechmere_Viaduct "Lechmere Viaduct"), including the [Science Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Science_Park_(MBTA_station) "Science Park (MBTA station)") and [Lechmere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lechmere_station "Lechmere station") stations, and a short segment of the [Red Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_Line_(MBTA) "Red Line (MBTA)") at [Charles-MGH](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles-MGH_(MBTA_station) "Charles-MGH (MBTA station)"), connecting the tunnel under [Beacon Hill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beacon_Hill,_Boston,_Massachusetts "Beacon Hill, Boston, Massachusetts") to the [Longfellow Bridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Longfellow_Bridge "Longfellow Bridge").

The [Boston Elevated Railway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston_Elevated_Railway "Boston Elevated Railway") was the company that owned all the elevateds and subways. The following Els once existed:

*   [Causeway Street Elevated](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Causeway_Street_Elevated "Causeway Street Elevated") (closed 2004), from the [Haymarket Incline](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haymarket_Incline "Haymarket Incline") to the [Lechmere Viaduct](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lechmere_Viaduct "Lechmere Viaduct")
*   [Washington Street Elevated](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_Street_Elevated "Washington Street Elevated") (closed 1987), from [Forest Hills](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forest_Hills_(MBTA_station) "Forest Hills (MBTA station)") to an incline north of the [Masspike](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masspike "Masspike")
*   [Charlestown Elevated](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charlestown_Elevated "Charlestown Elevated") (closed April 4, 1975), from the [Haymarket Incline](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haymarket_Incline "Haymarket Incline") to [Everett](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Everett,_Massachusetts "Everett, Massachusetts")
*   [Atlantic Avenue Elevated](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlantic_Avenue_Elevated "Atlantic Avenue Elevated") (closed 1938), from the Washington Street El at the [Castle Street Wye](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Castle_Street_Wye?action=edit&redlink=1 "Castle Street Wye (page does not exist)") at Herald Street (Tower 'D') to the Charlestown El and Causeway Street El at [North Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Station "North Station") (Tower 'C')

### Common user rail network

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Transportation_in_Boston&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Common user rail network")]

Unlike the subway, which is owned and operated by the MBTA, the common user network is owned and operated by a mixture of various public and private sector bodies. In the Boston area, trackage is owned by a mixture of the MBTA and several freight railroads. Commuter rail services are operated by the [Keolis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keolis "Keolis") Commuter Services (KCS)[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transportation_in_Boston#cite_note-39) under contract to the MBTA, intercity passenger services are operated by [Amtrak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amtrak "Amtrak"), and freight services are operated by the various freight railroads. [Trackage rights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trackage_rights "Trackage rights") allow trains of one operator to make use of tracks owned by another.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transportation_in_Boston#cite_note-sppnemc-40)

#### Commuter rail

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Transportation_in_Boston&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Commuter rail")]

Main article: [MBTA commuter rail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MBTA_commuter_rail "MBTA commuter rail")

[![Image 16](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/cb/Wellesley_Hills_station.jpg/250px-Wellesley_Hills_station.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Wellesley_Hills_station.jpg)

Commuter Rail train at Wellesley Hills

The MBTA commuter rail system brings people from as far away as [Worcester](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Worcester,_Massachusetts "Worcester, Massachusetts") and [Providence (Rhode Island)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Providence,_Rhode_Island "Providence, Rhode Island") into Boston. There are approximately 125,000 one-way trips on the commuter rail each day, making it the [fifth-busiest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_United_States_commuter_rail_systems_by_ridership "List of United States commuter rail systems by ridership") commuter rail system in the country, outranked only by the various systems serving New York and Chicago suburbs.

There are two major [rail terminals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rail_terminal "Rail terminal") in Boston: [North Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Station "North Station") and [South Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Station "South Station"). Commuter rail lines from the North Shore and northwestern suburbs begin and terminate at North Station; lines from the South Shore and the west start and end at South Station. There is no direct rail connection between North Station and South Station, so that interchange between the two stations generally requires the use of two different subway lines (Red/Orange or Red/Green). However, passengers on commuter lines serving [Back Bay Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Back_Bay_(MBTA_station) "Back Bay (MBTA station)") can interchange directly from there to North Station using the Orange Line, and passengers on the [Fitchburg Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fitchburg_Line "Fitchburg Line") can interchange directly from [Porter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Porter_(MBTA_station) "Porter (MBTA station)") to South Station using the Red Line.

#### Intercity rail

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Transportation_in_Boston&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Intercity rail")]

[![Image 17](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e2/Amtrak_623_%26_Acela_2007_at_South_Station_2019_jeh.jpg/250px-Amtrak_623_%26_Acela_2007_at_South_Station_2019_jeh.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Amtrak_623_&_Acela_2007_at_South_Station_2019_jeh.jpg)

_Acela_ (left) and _Northeast Regional_ (right) locomotives at South Station in 2019

Boston is served by four intercity rail services, all operated by [Amtrak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amtrak "Amtrak"). The _[Acela](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Acela "Acela")_ and _[Northeast Regional](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northeast\_Regional "Northeast Regional")_ services both operate on the [Northeast Corridor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northeast_Corridor "Northeast Corridor") to and from [Washington, D.C.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington,_D.C. "Washington, D.C."), with stops in places such as [New York City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City "New York City") and [Philadelphia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philadelphia "Philadelphia"). A branch of the _[Lake Shore Limited](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake\_Shore\_Limited "Lake Shore Limited")_ service operates to and from [Chicago](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago "Chicago"). The _[Downeaster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Downeaster\_(train) "Downeaster (train)")_ service operates to and from [Brunswick, Maine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brunswick,_Maine "Brunswick, Maine").[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transportation_in_Boston#cite_note-amra-41)

The Northeast Corridor services terminate at South Station, as does the _Lake Shore Limited_. The _Downeaster_ service terminates at North Station, primarily because the _Downeaster_ Amtrak line is intended for points north of downtown. The Northeast Corridor and _Lake Shore Limited_ services also stop at [Back Bay station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Back_Bay_station "Back Bay station"). The lack of a direct rail connection between North Station and South Station means that passengers transferring to and from the _Downeaster_ are faced with a transfer between stations. Although most such transfers can be achieved using the [Orange Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orange_Line_(MBTA) "Orange Line (MBTA)") between Back Bay and North Station, Amtrak recommends passengers with luggage to use a taxi.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transportation_in_Boston#cite_note-amra-41)[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transportation_in_Boston#cite_note-amrade-42)

Within the Boston area, most Amtrak services operate over commuter rail track owned by the MBTA, who also own the Northeast Corridor track as far as the [Rhode Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhode_Island "Rhode Island") state line.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transportation_in_Boston#cite_note-sppnemc-40)

### Major transit hubs

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Transportation_in_Boston&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Major transit hubs")]

There are several major transit terminals in the Boston metropolitan area.

Major rail stations include:

*   [South Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Station "South Station"), which is served by [Amtrak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amtrak "Amtrak") and [MBTA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MBTA "MBTA") commuter trains and subways, and intercity buses via the adjacent bus terminal
*   [North Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Station "North Station"), which is served by Amtrak and MBTA commuter trains and subways

#### Freight rail

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Transportation_in_Boston&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Freight rail")]

[CSX](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CSX_Transportation "CSX Transportation") is the only [class I railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Class_I_railroad "Class I railroad") serving the Boston area, which it reaches by its [Boston Subdivision](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston_Subdivision "Boston Subdivision") line to [Springfield](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Springfield,_Massachusetts "Springfield, Massachusetts"), and by [trackage rights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trackage_rights "Trackage rights") over the Northeast Corridor. CSX also has trackage rights over much of the southern half of the MBTA's commuter rail network. In February 2013, CSX moved freight operations from its Beacon Park Yard in [Allston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Allston,_Massachusetts "Allston, Massachusetts")[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transportation_in_Boston#cite_note-sppnemc-40) to a newly refurbished [double stack intermodal yard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Double-stack_rail_transport "Double-stack rail transport") in [Worcester](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Worcester,_Massachusetts "Worcester, Massachusetts") and a new [transload](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transload "Transload") facility in [Westborough](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Westborough,_Massachusetts "Westborough, Massachusetts").[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transportation_in_Boston#cite_note-43)

The other significant freight railroad in the Boston area is [Pan Am Railways](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pan_Am_Railways "Pan Am Railways") (PAR; formerly known as the Guilford Rail System). PAR is a [class II railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Class_II_railroad "Class II railroad") that operates lines to the north and west of Boston, reaching destinations in [New Hampshire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Hampshire "New Hampshire"), [Maine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maine "Maine") and [New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_(state) "New York (state)") as well as Massachusetts. It also has trackage rights over much of the northern half of the MBTA's commuter rail network. In May 2008, PAR announced a venture with [Norfolk Southern Railway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norfolk_Southern_Railway "Norfolk Southern Railway") to create a jointly owned freight corridor, branded the [Patriot Corridor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patriot_Corridor "Patriot Corridor"), linking Boston to a newly refurbished intermodal yard in [Mechanicville, New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mechanicville,_New_York "Mechanicville, New York"), just north of [Albany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albany,_New_York "Albany, New York").[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transportation_in_Boston#cite_note-sppnemc-40)[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transportation_in_Boston#cite_note-parnspc-44)

Only a few rail freight customers remain in or near Boston, including a chemical packager in Allston, and food distribution facilities and a scrap metal processor in [Everett](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Everett,_Massachusetts "Everett, Massachusetts"). The Class III [Fore River Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fore_River_Railroad "Fore River Railroad") serves two major customers in [Quincy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quincy,_Massachusetts "Quincy, Massachusetts"). A plan to ship [ethanol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethanol "Ethanol") by rail to a gasoline mixing plant in [Revere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Revere,_Massachusetts "Revere, Massachusetts") was reviewed in 2013.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transportation_in_Boston#cite_note-45)[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transportation_in_Boston#cite_note-46)[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transportation_in_Boston#cite_note-47) In the face of community opposition and pressure from the state legislature, the company withdrew its proposal on July 2, days before the [Lac-Mégantic derailment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lac-M%C3%A9gantic_derailment "Lac-Mégantic derailment").[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transportation_in_Boston#cite_note-48)

## Water transportation

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Transportation_in_Boston&action=edit&section=15 "Edit section: Water transportation")]

### Port of Boston

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Transportation_in_Boston&action=edit&section=16 "Edit section: Port of Boston")]

[![Image 18](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/5f/Boston_Long_Wharf.JPG/250px-Boston_Long_Wharf.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Boston_Long_Wharf.JPG)

[Long Wharf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Long_Wharf_(Boston) "Long Wharf (Boston)") in waterfront downtown Boston was once the main commercial wharf of the port, but is now used by ferries and cruise boats.

Main article: [Port of Boston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Port_of_Boston "Port of Boston")

The Port of Boston is a major [seaport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seaport "Seaport") and the largest port in [Massachusetts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massachusetts "Massachusetts"). It was historically important for the growth of the city, and was originally located in what is now the downtown area of the city. Land reclamation and conversion to other uses means that downtown area no longer handles commercial traffic, although the [US Coast Guard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Coast_Guard "United States Coast Guard") maintains a major base there, and there is still considerable ferry and leisure usage.

Today the principal cargo handling facilities are located in the Boston neighborhoods of [Charlestown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charlestown,_Massachusetts "Charlestown, Massachusetts"), [East Boston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Boston "East Boston"), and [South Boston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Boston "South Boston"), and in the neighbouring city of [Everett](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Everett,_Massachusetts "Everett, Massachusetts"). In 2011, the port handled over 11.5 million [metric tons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metric_ton "Metric ton") of cargo, including 192,000 [container](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Containerization "Containerization")[TEUs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Twenty-foot_equivalent_unit "Twenty-foot equivalent unit"). Other major forms of cargo processed at the port include [petroleum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Petroleum "Petroleum"), [liquefied natural gas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liquefied_natural_gas "Liquefied natural gas") (LNG), [automobiles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Automobile "Automobile"), [cement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cement "Cement"), [gypsum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gypsum "Gypsum"), and [salt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salt "Salt").[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transportation_in_Boston#cite_note-stats-49)

The _[Black Falcon Cruise Terminal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black\_Falcon\_Cruise\_Terminal "Black Falcon Cruise Terminal")_ situated in South Boston, was renovated and expanded in 2010. [[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transportation_in_Boston#cite_note-bfct-50) During 2012, it served 117 ships and more than 380,000 passengers.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transportation_in_Boston#cite_note-51)

### Passenger boat services

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Transportation_in_Boston&action=edit&section=17 "Edit section: Passenger boat services")]

[![Image 19](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b8/Boston_water_taxis.jpg/250px-Boston_water_taxis.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Boston_water_taxis.jpg)

A pair of water taxis operating on the waterfront of Boston

The [MBTA ferry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MBTA_ferry "MBTA ferry") system comprises several [ferry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferry "Ferry") routes on [Boston Harbor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston_Harbor "Boston Harbor"). The system has eight routes that terminate in downtown Boston. Year-round routes run to [Hingham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hingham,_Massachusetts "Hingham, Massachusetts") directly (F1) and via [Hull](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hull,_Massachusetts "Hull, Massachusetts") (F2H), and to the [Charlestown Navy Yard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston_Navy_Yard "Boston Navy Yard") (F4). Seasonal routes run to [East Boston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Boston "East Boston") (F3), [Lynn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lynn,_Massachusetts "Lynn, Massachusetts") (F5), [Winthrop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Winthrop,_Massachusetts "Winthrop, Massachusetts") (F6), and [Quincy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quincy,_Massachusetts "Quincy, Massachusetts") (F7); combined Winthrop/Quincy weekend service operates as F8. All services are operated by [private sector](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Private_sector "Private sector") companies under contract to the MBTA.

Outside the MBTA system, seasonal passenger ferry services operate to the [Boston Harbor Islands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston_Harbor_Islands_National_Recreation_Area "Boston Harbor Islands National Recreation Area"), to the city of [Salem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salem,_Massachusetts "Salem, Massachusetts") north of Boston, and to the town of [Provincetown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Provincetown,_Massachusetts "Provincetown, Massachusetts") on [Cape Cod](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cape_Cod "Cape Cod"). [Water taxis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Water_taxi "Water taxi") provide on-demand service from various points on the downtown waterfront and from [Logan Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Logan_International_Airport "Logan International Airport"), and in particular between the airport and downtown.

Several companies operate tourist oriented cruise boats on the harbor and on the [Charles River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_River "Charles River"). Other companies operate [duck tours](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duck_tour "Duck tour") that use amphibious vehicles (mostly derived from World War II era [DUKWs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DUKW "DUKW")), and encompass both the city's streets and its waterways.

## Commuting statistics

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Transportation_in_Boston&action=edit&section=18 "Edit section: Commuting statistics")]

The average amount of time people spend commuting with public transit in Boston, for example to and from work, on a weekday is 83 min. 29% of public transit riders ride for more than two hours every day. The average amount of time people wait at a stop or station for public transit is 15 minutes, while 24% of riders wait for over 20 minutes on average every day. The average distance people usually ride in a single trip with public transit is 7 km, while 12% travel for over 12 km in a single direction.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transportation_in_Boston#cite_note-52)

In 2013, the Boston-Cambridge-Newton metropolitan statistical area (Boston MSA) had the seventh-lowest percentage of workers who commuted by private automobile (75.6 percent), with 6.2 percent of area workers traveling via rail transit. During the period starting in 2006 and ending in 2013, the Boston MSA had the greatest percentage decline of workers commuting by automobile (3.3 percent) among MSAs with more than a half-million residents.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transportation_in_Boston#cite_note-53)

In 2019, a yearly ranking of time wasted in traffic listed Boston area drivers lost approximately 164 hours a year in lost productivity due to the area's traffic congestion. This amounted to $2,300 a year per driver in costs.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transportation_in_Boston#cite_note-54)

## Aviation

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Transportation_in_Boston&action=edit&section=19 "Edit section: Aviation")]

See also: [Massachusetts Port Authority](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massachusetts_Port_Authority "Massachusetts Port Authority") and [List of airports in Massachusetts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_airports_in_Massachusetts "List of airports in Massachusetts")

[![Image 20](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/16/Logan_Airport_aerial_view.jpg/250px-Logan_Airport_aerial_view.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Logan_Airport_aerial_view.jpg)

An aerial photograph of Logan International Airport

Boston's principal airport is [Logan International Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Logan_International_Airport "Logan International Airport") ([BOS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Air_Transport_Association_airport_code "International Air Transport Association airport code")), situated in [East Boston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Boston,_Massachusetts "East Boston, Massachusetts") just across inner [Boston Harbor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston_Harbor "Boston Harbor") from downtown Boston. Logan Airport is operated by the [Massachusetts Port Authority](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massachusetts_Port_Authority "Massachusetts Port Authority") (Massport) and has extensive domestic and international airline service. The airport is linked to downtown by several highway tunnels. The [Silver Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silver_Line_(MBTA) "Silver Line (MBTA)")[bus rapid transit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bus_rapid_transit "Bus rapid transit") uses these tunnels to connect Logan's terminals with [South Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Station "South Station"). There are also shuttle buses between the terminals and the [Blue Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Line_(MBTA) "Blue Line (MBTA)")[Airport station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Airport_(MBTA_station) "Airport (MBTA station)").

To help address overcrowding at Logan Airport, Massport operates two other airports in eastern Massachusetts:

*   [L.G. Hanscom Field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hanscom_Field "Hanscom Field")
*   [Worcester Regional Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Worcester_Regional_Airport "Worcester Regional Airport"): formerly owned by the city of [Worcester](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Worcester,_Massachusetts "Worcester, Massachusetts") until ownership transfer to Massport was mandated by law in 2009,[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transportation_in_Boston#cite_note-55) and subsequently completed on June 22, 2010.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transportation_in_Boston#cite_note-56)

In addition, MassPort has designated two out of state regional airports (which are administered independently) as reliever airports:[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transportation_in_Boston#cite_note-57)

*   [T. F. Green Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhode_Island_T._F._Green_International_Airport "Rhode Island T. F. Green International Airport") near [Providence, Rhode Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Providence,_Rhode_Island "Providence, Rhode Island")
*   [Manchester-Boston Regional Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manchester-Boston_Regional_Airport "Manchester-Boston Regional Airport") in [Manchester, New Hampshire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manchester,_New_Hampshire "Manchester, New Hampshire")

There are also several [general aviation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_aviation "General aviation") facilities for private planes in the Boston area, including [Beverly Regional Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beverly_Regional_Airport "Beverly Regional Airport") and [Lawrence Municipal Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lawrence_Municipal_Airport_(Massachusetts) "Lawrence Municipal Airport (Massachusetts)") to the north, Hanscom Field to the west, and [Norwood Memorial Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norwood_Memorial_Airport "Norwood Memorial Airport") to the south.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transportation_in_Boston#cite_note-58)

Since the [September 11, 2001 attacks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/September_11,_2001_attacks "September 11, 2001 attacks"), strict security has been implemented at all of Boston's airports. Because of this and its location as the closest American port to Europe, Boston is an emergency destination for airliners that experience security or mechanical problems while en route to the US, although they may also be diverted to [Halifax, Nova Scotia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Halifax,_Nova_Scotia "Halifax, Nova Scotia"), or other Canadian airports.

## Boston Vision Zero Plan

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Transportation_in_Boston&action=edit&section=20 "Edit section: Boston Vision Zero Plan")]

In 2015, mayor [Marty Walsh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marty_Walsh "Marty Walsh") announced that the city of [Boston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston "Boston") would become part of a worldwide program known as [Vision Zero](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vision_Zero "Vision Zero").[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transportation_in_Boston#cite_note-:0-59) Vision Zero is a plan self described as “a new standard for safety on our streets.” The plan aims to eliminate deaths caused by transportation, whether that be pedestrians, personal vehicle riders, or cyclists.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transportation_in_Boston#cite_note-60)

Since 2015, the city of Boston has adopted several different policies aimed to help bring down the number of fatalities caused by Transportation in Boston. These policies include the creation of a 25-mile per hour speed limit law citywide,[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transportation_in_Boston#cite_note-:1-61) and the implementation of Neighborhood Slow Streets, a tool of [Traffic calming](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Traffic_calming "Traffic calming") designed to make personal vehicles slow down in residential areas.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transportation_in_Boston#cite_note-62) Pedestrian deaths have fallen to 57 in 2019, down from the 2017 total of 82. Cyclist deaths have also fallen from 10 in 2017 to just 3 in 2019.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transportation_in_Boston#cite_note-63)

Boston now seeks to expand this plan by committing more funds to the program, as they currently spend roughly five dollars per person annually on the Vision Zero plan, whereas cities like San Francisco spend upwards of seventy five dollars per person annually.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transportation_in_Boston#cite_note-:1-61) Boston aims to eliminate vehicle crash fatalities by 2030, while planning for more Neighborhood Slow Streets, speed humps, and curb extensions to help bring vehicle fatalities down to zero.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transportation_in_Boston#cite_note-:0-59) One area that the Boston Transportation Department specifically wants to focus on are the numerous Boston public schools, stating in their 2017/2018 vision zero report, that “We will be upgrading school zone flashers throughout the City and focusing on schools as we select locations for future safety improvements.” [[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transportation_in_Boston#cite_note-:0-59)
