[Dallas Area Rapid Transit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dallas_Area_Rapid_Transit "Dallas Area Rapid Transit") (DART) is the Dallas area public transportation authority, providing bus and rail service.

DART began operating the first [light rail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Light_rail "Light rail") system in the [Southwest United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southwest_United_States "Southwest United States") in 1996 and continues to expand its coverage. Currently, four [light rail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DART_rail "DART rail") lines and one [hybrid rail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hybrid_rail "Hybrid rail") line are in service. The [Red Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_Line_(DART) "Red Line (DART)") goes through [Oak Cliff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oak_Cliff "Oak Cliff"), [downtown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Downtown_Dallas "Downtown Dallas"), [Uptown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uptown_Dallas "Uptown Dallas"), [North Dallas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Dallas "North Dallas"), [Richardson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richardson,_Texas "Richardson, Texas") and [Plano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plano,_Texas "Plano, Texas"). The [Blue Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Line_(DART) "Blue Line (DART)") goes through [South Dallas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Dallas "South Dallas"), downtown, Uptown, North Dallas, [Garland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Garland,_Texas "Garland, Texas"), and [Rowlett](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rowlett,_Texas "Rowlett, Texas"). The [Green Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Line_(DART) "Green Line (DART)") goes through south east Dallas, [Fair Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fair_Park "Fair Park"), [Baylor University Medical Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baylor_University_Medical_Center "Baylor University Medical Center"), downtown, [Victory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victory_station "Victory station"), west of [Dallas Love Field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dallas_Love_Field "Dallas Love Field"), Farmers Branch, then ends in [Carrollton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carrollton,_Texas "Carrollton, Texas"). The [Orange Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orange_Line_(DART) "Orange Line (DART)") follows the DART Red Line from North Plano through downtown, then follows the Green Line up through Victory, to Bachman Station, then goes west to [Las Colinas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Las_Colinas "Las Colinas") before terminating at [DFW Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DFW_Airport "DFW Airport"). The [Silver Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silver_Line_(DART) "Silver Line (DART)") goes through [Grapevine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grapevine,_Texas "Grapevine, Texas"), Carrollton, [Addison](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Addison,_Texas "Addison, Texas"), Richardson, and Plano. All current rail lines are connected downtown by four rail stations. Red, Orange and Blue Lines connect to [Cityplace/Uptown Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cityplace/Uptown_(DART_station) "Cityplace/Uptown (DART station)"), currently the only subway station in the Southwest.

The [M-Line Trolley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M-Line_Trolley "M-Line Trolley"), a [heritage streetcar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heritage_streetcar "Heritage streetcar"), provides service between [Cityplace/Uptown station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cityplace/Uptown_station "Cityplace/Uptown station") in [Uptown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uptown,_Dallas "Uptown, Dallas") and [St Paul station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Paul_station_(DART) "St. Paul station (DART)") in [Downtown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Downtown_Dallas "Downtown Dallas").

DART completed expansions to the Orange line in 2014, bringing the length of the light rail system to around 93 miles (150 km). Further ambitions include expanding the commuter rail network in the region to over 93 miles (150 km); expanding the DART rail network to over 150 miles (240 km) with a second route through downtown included; expanding the [Dallas Streetcar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dallas_Streetcar "Dallas Streetcar") to the Bishop Arts District and Convention Center Hotel; and expanding the elevated [Las Colinas Area Personal Transit system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Las_Colinas_APT_System "Las Colinas APT System") to serve new entertainment venues in the area.

The [DART rail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DART_rail "DART rail") system remained the only light rail system in Texas until [Houston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Houston,_Texas "Houston, Texas") opened [METRORail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/METRORail "METRORail"), its starter light rail system (one line running less than 10 miles), in 2004. Fort Worth's smaller public transit system connects with Dallas's via a commuter rail line, the [Trinity Railway Express](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trinity_Railway_Express "Trinity Railway Express"), connecting downtown Dallas's [Union Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Union_Station_(Dallas) "Union Station (Dallas)") with downtown Fort Worth's [T&P Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/T&P_Station "T&P Station") and several points in between. The light rail system has caused a dramatic increase in land values in downtown Dallas and has sparked a residential population boom in the area. Although the system is increasingly popular, large parts of the Metroplex remain outside the current service area of the system and remain dependent on the automobile.

DART now uses Google Maps as its main provider of transit information. An independent company, [Dadnab](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dadnab "Dadnab"), offers a service that enables riders to retrieve similar information using text messaging from their mobile phones. DART provides transit route and schedule information to Google and this has spawned a new generation of trip planners such as [TransitTrips](https://web.archive.org/web/20080927230139/http://transittrips.com/).

## Dallas Union Station rail service

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Transportation_in_Dallas&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Dallas Union Station rail service")]

[Amtrak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amtrak "Amtrak")'s _[Texas Eagle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas\_Eagle "Texas Eagle")_ train makes a stop at the [Dallas Union Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dallas_Union_Station "Dallas Union Station"). Its eastern terminus is [Chicago, Illinois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago,_Illinois "Chicago, Illinois"). Its western terminus is [San Antonio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Antonio "San Antonio"), however, sleeping car passengers have continuing service on the _[Sunset Limited](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sunset\_Limited "Sunset Limited"),_ to [Los Angeles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles "Los Angeles"). The station also is a transfer point for the aforementioned DART light rail and Trinity Railway Express commuter rail.

## Airports

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Transportation_in_Dallas&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Airports")]

[![Image 13](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6e/Dfw_airport.jpg/250px-Dfw_airport.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Dfw_airport.jpg)

[Dallas/Fort Worth International Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dallas/Fort_Worth_International_Airport "Dallas/Fort Worth International Airport") serves most [passengers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Passengers "Passengers") flying in and out of the [metroplex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dallas/Fort_Worth_Metroplex "Dallas/Fort Worth Metroplex")

Dallas is served by two commercial [airports](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Airports "Airports"): [Dallas/Fort Worth International Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dallas/Fort_Worth_International_Airport "Dallas/Fort Worth International Airport") (known as DFW International) and [Dallas Love Field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dallas_Love_Field "Dallas Love Field"). In addition, [Dallas Executive Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dallas_Executive_Airport "Dallas Executive Airport") (formerly Redbird Airport), is a [general aviation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_aviation "General aviation") airport located within the city limits, and [Addison Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Addison_Airport "Addison Airport") is another general aviation airport located just outside the city limits in the [suburb](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suburb "Suburb") of [Addison](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Addison,_Texas "Addison, Texas"). Another general aviation airport, [Denton Municipal Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denton_Municipal_Airport "Denton Municipal Airport") is located 40 miles (64 km) northwest of Dallas in [Denton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denton,_Texas "Denton, Texas"). Two more general aviation airports are located in the outer suburb of [McKinney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/McKinney,_Texas "McKinney, Texas"), and on the west side of the Metroplex, two general aviation airports are located in [Fort Worth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Worth,_Texas "Fort Worth, Texas").

[DFW International Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dallas/Fort_Worth_International_Airport "Dallas/Fort Worth International Airport") is located in the suburbs north of and equidistant to downtown [Fort Worth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Worth "Fort Worth") and downtown Dallas. In terms of size, DFW is the largest airport in the state, the second largest in the United States, and third largest in the world. In terms of traffic, DFW is the busiest in the state, third busiest in the United States, and sixth busiest in the world. DFW is also home base to [American Airlines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Airlines "American Airlines"), formerly the world's largest [airline](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Airline "Airline") which operates eighty-four percent of all passenger traffic at the airport. _[Air Cargo World](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Air\_Cargo\_World "Air Cargo World")_ named DFW "_The Best Cargo Airport in the World_" on 7 March 2006.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transportation_in_Dallas#cite_note-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transportation_in_Dallas#cite_note-7)

[Love Field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dallas_Love_Field "Dallas Love Field") is located within the city limits of Dallas, 6 miles (10 km) northwest of downtown, and is headquarters to [Southwest Airlines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southwest_Airlines "Southwest Airlines"). Under the Federal "[Wright Amendment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wright_Amendment "Wright Amendment")" and "Shelby Amendment" laws, no large jet air service was allowed before 2014 from Dallas Love Field to any point beyond Texas, [Louisiana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louisiana "Louisiana"), [Arkansas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arkansas "Arkansas"), [Oklahoma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oklahoma "Oklahoma"), [New Mexico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Mexico "New Mexico"), [Kansas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kansas "Kansas"), [Mississippi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mississippi "Mississippi"), [Alabama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alabama "Alabama"), and [Missouri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Missouri "Missouri"). However, the amendment was entirely repealed in an all-party compromise that took effect in 2014, and Love Field is now able to service any city in America.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transportation_in_Dallas#cite_note-8)

## Walking and bicycling

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Transportation_in_Dallas&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Walking and bicycling")]

[![Image 5](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/cb/Stone_Street_near_the_Main_Street_District_of_downtown_Dallas.jpg/250px-Stone_Street_near_the_Main_Street_District_of_downtown_Dallas.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Stone_Street_near_the_Main_Street_District_of_downtown_Dallas.jpg)

Pedestrians along Stone Street, near the [Main Street](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Main_Street,_Dallas,_Texas "Main Street, Dallas, Texas") corridor of downtown Dallas.

Dallas is the 30th most walkable large city in the US, with a [Walk Score](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walk_Score "Walk Score") of 47.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transportation_in_Dallas#cite_note-1) Most of the pedestrian-friendly areas in the city are near [downtown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Downtown_Dallas "Downtown Dallas") and [Uptown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uptown_Dallas "Uptown Dallas"). The majority of Dallas, whether or not it was developed with the pedestrian in mind, was completely rebuilt or reworked to accommodate the vehicle in the mid-20th century. In the late 1990s and early 2000s (decade), the importance of the pedestrian, bicyclist, and those who use mass transportation began to be realized and most new developments cater to all forms of transportation.

Walking trails, though once nonexistent, are also starting to be built and improved by the city. Perhaps the flagship is the [Katy Trail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Katy_Trail_(Dallas) "Katy Trail (Dallas)"), built over the old Katy Railway, which goes from the [Victory Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victory_Park,_Dallas,_Texas "Victory Park, Dallas, Texas") neighborhood through [Uptown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uptown_Dallas "Uptown Dallas") and [Oak Lawn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oak_Lawn,_Dallas,_Texas "Oak Lawn, Dallas, Texas") up to [Knox Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Knox_Park,_Dallas,_Texas "Knox Park, Dallas, Texas"). Other trails include the levee-top trails along the [Trinity River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trinity_River_(Texas) "Trinity River (Texas)") and the [Texas Buckeye Trail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Buckeye_Trail?action=edit&redlink=1 "Texas Buckeye Trail (page does not exist)") in the [Great Trinity Forest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Trinity_Forest "Great Trinity Forest") of [south Dallas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Dallas "South Dallas"). The city also maintains walking trails at area parks including parks around [White Rock Lake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Rock_Lake "White Rock Lake") and [Bachman Lake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bachman_Lake "Bachman Lake").

The city maintains 800 lane miles of cyclist-selected bike routes along low-volume roadways throughout the city that parallel major thoroughfares. The City does not employ bicycle control devices like bike lanes, as the necessary pre-conditions do not exist. The city has also installed a series of Pedestrian Tunnels in Downtown Dallas, although these have been under much criticism regarding their ability to "suck the life off of" the aboveground streets.

## Streets

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Transportation_in_Dallas&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Streets")]

[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d4/Dallas%2C_Texas_Map_1905.jpg/250px-Dallas%2C_Texas_Map_1905.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Dallas,_Texas_Map_1905.jpg)

A 1905 map showing several early street grid attempts

[![Image 7](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b6/Dallas%2C_Texas_road_map.svg/250px-Dallas%2C_Texas_road_map.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Dallas,_Texas_road_map.svg)

Major and minor thoroughfares in Dallas and its enclaves

Dallas is devoid of any major street grid as a whole, though a number of major attempts intersect at awkward angles and in confusing interchanges around the city. The main street grid in the center city runs 45° to the typical N/S/E/W grid, creating confusion for many out-of-town visitors. This street grid prevails primarily in [east Dallas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Dallas "East Dallas"), though it also permeates [Oak Lawn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oak_Lawn,_Dallas,_Texas "Oak Lawn, Dallas, Texas"), portions of [downtown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Downtown_Dallas "Downtown Dallas"), and the [Cedars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cedars,_Dallas,_Texas "Cedars, Dallas, Texas"). Another much smaller street grid lies downtown between Pacific and Young streets — it is about 15° off the typical N/S/E/W grid, and is on average 5-8 streets across N/S and about 3 miles (5 km) wide E/W. There is also a fairly extensive N/S/E/W grid around the original city of [Oak Cliff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oak_Cliff "Oak Cliff"). The rest of Dallas, developed from the middle of the 20th century on, is typically on a N/S/E/W grid, especially with major thoroughfares. In trying to make the city traversable, city planners have over time created wide boulevards that jump between the rights-of-way of multiple minor streets, trying to force a wide road wherever they can discover space for it. This forces the destruction of the minor streets' original paths, a name-change for the boulevard or minor streets, and roads (e.g. [Cole 1](https://maps.google.com/maps?f=d&hl=en&saddr=Cole+Ave+%26+N+Fitzhugh+Ave,+Dallas,+TX+75205&daddr=cole+at+cedar+springs,+dallas,+tx&ie=UTF8&ll=32.807007,-96.798778&spn=0.027486,0.057335&om=1), [2](https://maps.google.com/maps?f=d&hl=en&saddr=Cole+Ave+%26+hall+st,+Dallas,+TX+75204&daddr=cole+at+cedar+springs,+dallas,+tx&ie=UTF8&om=1), [3](https://maps.google.com/maps?f=d&hl=en&saddr=Cole+St+%26+N+Industrial+Blvd,+Dallas,+TX+75207&daddr=Cole+St+%26+E+Levee+St,+Dallas,+TX+75207&ie=UTF8&om=1)) that exist in two or more places. Major thoroughfares in Oak Cliff typically do not cross the [Trinity River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trinity_River_(Texas) "Trinity River (Texas)"), and when they do, they frequently do not continue with the same name on the north or eastern sides, which creates a degree of confusion. Also, many times a street will change names each time it crosses a municipal border. Conversely, many streets keep their names through sharp turns across the city.

## Highways

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Transportation_in_Dallas&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Highways")]

[![Image 8](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d0/Southbound_I-45_at_Dallas_North_Central_Expressway.jpg/250px-Southbound_I-45_at_Dallas_North_Central_Expressway.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Southbound_I-45_at_Dallas_North_Central_Expressway.jpg)

[North Central Expressway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Expressway_(Dallas) "Central Expressway (Dallas)") southbound towards downtown Dallas

See also: [List of Dallas freeways](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Dallas_freeways "List of Dallas freeways")

The city of Dallas is at the confluence of a large number of major [interstate highways](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interstate_highway_system "Interstate highway system")—Interstates [20](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interstate_20_(Texas) "Interstate 20 (Texas)"), [30](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interstate_30_(Texas) "Interstate 30 (Texas)"), [35E](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interstate_35E_(Texas) "Interstate 35E (Texas)"), and [45](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interstate_45_(Texas) "Interstate 45 (Texas)") all run through the city. The city's freeway system, as it has no major geographical inhibitors surrounding it, is set up in the popular [hub-and-spoke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spoke-hub_distribution_paradigm "Spoke-hub distribution paradigm") system, much like a wagon wheel. The center of the system is the downtown freeway loop, made up of Interstate 30 on the south, Interstate 35E on the west, [Spur 366](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_State_Highway_Spur_366 "Texas State Highway Spur 366") on the north, and [Interstate 345](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interstate_345_(Texas) "Interstate 345 (Texas)") on the east. (Interstate 345 is a short spur of Interstate 45 that connects Interstate 45 with [US 75](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Highway_75_(Texas) "U.S. Highway 75 (Texas)").) The next major freeway loop is the [Interstate 635](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interstate_635_(Texas) "Interstate 635 (Texas)")/[20](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interstate_20_(Texas) "Interstate 20 (Texas)") Lyndon B. Johnson loop, and the outermost is the tolled [President George Bush Turnpike](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_George_Bush_Turnpike "President George Bush Turnpike"). Inside these freeway loops are other partially limited-access and parkway-style loops including [Loop 12](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_State_Highway_Loop_12 "Texas State Highway Loop 12") and Belt Line Road. Another beltway around the city is planned upwards of 45 miles (72 km) from downtown in [Collin County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Collin_County,_Texas "Collin County, Texas"). Radiating out of downtown as the spokes of the system are Interstates 30, 35E, and 45, [US 75](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Highway_75_(Texas) "U.S. Highway 75 (Texas)"), [US 175](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Highway_175_(Texas) "U.S. Highway 175 (Texas)"), [Spur 366](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_State_Highway_Spur_366 "Texas State Highway Spur 366"), the tolled [Dallas North Tollway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dallas_North_Tollway "Dallas North Tollway"), and further out [SH 114](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State_Highway_114_(Texas) "State Highway 114 (Texas)"), [US 80](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Highway_80_(Texas) "U.S. Highway 80 (Texas)") and [US 67](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Highway_67_(Texas) "U.S. Highway 67 (Texas)"). Other major highways within the city that do not serve primarily as spokes include [SH 183](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State_Highway_183_(Texas) "State Highway 183 (Texas)") and [Spur 408](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State_Highway_Spur_408_(Texas) "State Highway Spur 408 (Texas)").

Portions of Interstates 30, 35E, and 635, and US 75 also have either bidirectional or reversible [HOV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HOV "HOV") lanes. Future highway plans typically integrate usage of both HOV and/or HOT (tolled) lanes, e.g. the expansion of Interstate 635. Plans for the road include HOV lanes and massive HOT tunnels in the heavily congested segment of the highway between, generally, Interstate 35E and US 75. This portion of the highway travels through one of the densest regions of [north Dallas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Dallas "North Dallas"), which, coupled with its primary role as a circulator for commuters, makes the freeway constantly congested at all hours of the day and night.

The city of Dallas's freeways, much like the city, are generally relatively new and in good condition. [TxDOT](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Department_of_Transportation "Texas Department of Transportation") is famous for its highway system in the state and many of what could be considered "flagship freeways" lie within the city. One example is [North Central Expressway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Expressway_(Dallas) "Central Expressway (Dallas)") or [US 75](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Highway_75_(Texas) "U.S. Highway 75 (Texas)"), which was trenched, immaculately landscaped and heavily ornamented between downtown and Loop 12 in the 1990s. Interstate 30 west of downtown Dallas was recently brought to a level near North Central Expressway and Interstate 635, Interstate 30 east of downtown, and Interstate 35E all share similar futures. Construction, like many cities, is a constant burden for the city's heavily automobile-centered culture.

[Dallas Area Rapid Transit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dallas_Area_Rapid_Transit "Dallas Area Rapid Transit") (DART) is the Dallas area public transportation authority, providing bus and rail service.

DART began operating the first [light rail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Light_rail "Light rail") system in the [Southwest United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southwest_United_States "Southwest United States") in 1996 and continues to expand its coverage. Currently, four [light rail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DART_rail "DART rail") lines and one [hybrid rail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hybrid_rail "Hybrid rail") line are in service. The [Red Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_Line_(DART) "Red Line (DART)") goes through [Oak Cliff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oak_Cliff "Oak Cliff"), [downtown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Downtown_Dallas "Downtown Dallas"), [Uptown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uptown_Dallas "Uptown Dallas"), [North Dallas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Dallas "North Dallas"), [Richardson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richardson,_Texas "Richardson, Texas") and [Plano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plano,_Texas "Plano, Texas"). The [Blue Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Line_(DART) "Blue Line (DART)") goes through [South Dallas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Dallas "South Dallas"), downtown, Uptown, North Dallas, [Garland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Garland,_Texas "Garland, Texas"), and [Rowlett](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rowlett,_Texas "Rowlett, Texas"). The [Green Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Line_(DART) "Green Line (DART)") goes through south east Dallas, [Fair Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fair_Park "Fair Park"), [Baylor University Medical Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baylor_University_Medical_Center "Baylor University Medical Center"), downtown, [Victory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victory_station "Victory station"), west of [Dallas Love Field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dallas_Love_Field "Dallas Love Field"), Farmers Branch, then ends in [Carrollton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carrollton,_Texas "Carrollton, Texas"). The [Orange Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orange_Line_(DART) "Orange Line (DART)") follows the DART Red Line from North Plano through downtown, then follows the Green Line up through Victory, to Bachman Station, then goes west to [Las Colinas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Las_Colinas "Las Colinas") before terminating at [DFW Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DFW_Airport "DFW Airport"). The [Silver Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silver_Line_(DART) "Silver Line (DART)") goes through [Grapevine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grapevine,_Texas "Grapevine, Texas"), Carrollton, [Addison](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Addison,_Texas "Addison, Texas"), Richardson, and Plano. All current rail lines are connected downtown by four rail stations. Red, Orange and Blue Lines connect to [Cityplace/Uptown Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cityplace/Uptown_(DART_station) "Cityplace/Uptown (DART station)"), currently the only subway station in the Southwest.

The [M-Line Trolley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M-Line_Trolley "M-Line Trolley"), a [heritage streetcar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heritage_streetcar "Heritage streetcar"), provides service between [Cityplace/Uptown station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cityplace/Uptown_station "Cityplace/Uptown station") in [Uptown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uptown,_Dallas "Uptown, Dallas") and [St Paul station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Paul_station_(DART) "St. Paul station (DART)") in [Downtown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Downtown_Dallas "Downtown Dallas").

DART completed expansions to the Orange line in 2014, bringing the length of the light rail system to around 93 miles (150 km). Further ambitions include expanding the commuter rail network in the region to over 93 miles (150 km); expanding the DART rail network to over 150 miles (240 km) with a second route through downtown included; expanding the [Dallas Streetcar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dallas_Streetcar "Dallas Streetcar") to the Bishop Arts District and Convention Center Hotel; and expanding the elevated [Las Colinas Area Personal Transit system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Las_Colinas_APT_System "Las Colinas APT System") to serve new entertainment venues in the area.

The [DART rail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DART_rail "DART rail") system remained the only light rail system in Texas until [Houston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Houston,_Texas "Houston, Texas") opened [METRORail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/METRORail "METRORail"), its starter light rail system (one line running less than 10 miles), in 2004. Fort Worth's smaller public transit system connects with Dallas's via a commuter rail line, the [Trinity Railway Express](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trinity_Railway_Express "Trinity Railway Express"), connecting downtown Dallas's [Union Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Union_Station_(Dallas) "Union Station (Dallas)") with downtown Fort Worth's [T&P Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/T&P_Station "T&P Station") and several points in between. The light rail system has caused a dramatic increase in land values in downtown Dallas and has sparked a residential population boom in the area. Although the system is increasingly popular, large parts of the Metroplex remain outside the current service area of the system and remain dependent on the automobile.

DART now uses Google Maps as its main provider of transit information. An independent company, [Dadnab](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dadnab "Dadnab"), offers a service that enables riders to retrieve similar information using text messaging from their mobile phones. DART provides transit route and schedule information to Google and this has spawned a new generation of trip planners such as [TransitTrips](https://web.archive.org/web/20080927230139/http://transittrips.com/).

## Dallas Union Station rail service

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Transportation_in_Dallas&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Dallas Union Station rail service")]

[Amtrak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amtrak "Amtrak")'s _[Texas Eagle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas\_Eagle "Texas Eagle")_ train makes a stop at the [Dallas Union Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dallas_Union_Station "Dallas Union Station"). Its eastern terminus is [Chicago, Illinois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago,_Illinois "Chicago, Illinois"). Its western terminus is [San Antonio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Antonio "San Antonio"), however, sleeping car passengers have continuing service on the _[Sunset Limited](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sunset\_Limited "Sunset Limited"),_ to [Los Angeles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles "Los Angeles"). The station also is a transfer point for the aforementioned DART light rail and Trinity Railway Express commuter rail.

## Airports

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Transportation_in_Dallas&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Airports")]

[![Image 13](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6e/Dfw_airport.jpg/250px-Dfw_airport.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Dfw_airport.jpg)

[Dallas/Fort Worth International Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dallas/Fort_Worth_International_Airport "Dallas/Fort Worth International Airport") serves most [passengers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Passengers "Passengers") flying in and out of the [metroplex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dallas/Fort_Worth_Metroplex "Dallas/Fort Worth Metroplex")

Dallas is served by two commercial [airports](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Airports "Airports"): [Dallas/Fort Worth International Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dallas/Fort_Worth_International_Airport "Dallas/Fort Worth International Airport") (known as DFW International) and [Dallas Love Field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dallas_Love_Field "Dallas Love Field"). In addition, [Dallas Executive Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dallas_Executive_Airport "Dallas Executive Airport") (formerly Redbird Airport), is a [general aviation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_aviation "General aviation") airport located within the city limits, and [Addison Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Addison_Airport "Addison Airport") is another general aviation airport located just outside the city limits in the [suburb](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suburb "Suburb") of [Addison](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Addison,_Texas "Addison, Texas"). Another general aviation airport, [Denton Municipal Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denton_Municipal_Airport "Denton Municipal Airport") is located 40 miles (64 km) northwest of Dallas in [Denton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denton,_Texas "Denton, Texas"). Two more general aviation airports are located in the outer suburb of [McKinney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/McKinney,_Texas "McKinney, Texas"), and on the west side of the Metroplex, two general aviation airports are located in [Fort Worth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Worth,_Texas "Fort Worth, Texas").

[DFW International Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dallas/Fort_Worth_International_Airport "Dallas/Fort Worth International Airport") is located in the suburbs north of and equidistant to downtown [Fort Worth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Worth "Fort Worth") and downtown Dallas. In terms of size, DFW is the largest airport in the state, the second largest in the United States, and third largest in the world. In terms of traffic, DFW is the busiest in the state, third busiest in the United States, and sixth busiest in the world. DFW is also home base to [American Airlines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Airlines "American Airlines"), formerly the world's largest [airline](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Airline "Airline") which operates eighty-four percent of all passenger traffic at the airport. _[Air Cargo World](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Air\_Cargo\_World "Air Cargo World")_ named DFW "_The Best Cargo Airport in the World_" on 7 March 2006.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transportation_in_Dallas#cite_note-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transportation_in_Dallas#cite_note-7)

[Love Field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dallas_Love_Field "Dallas Love Field") is located within the city limits of Dallas, 6 miles (10 km) northwest of downtown, and is headquarters to [Southwest Airlines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southwest_Airlines "Southwest Airlines"). Under the Federal "[Wright Amendment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wright_Amendment "Wright Amendment")" and "Shelby Amendment" laws, no large jet air service was allowed before 2014 from Dallas Love Field to any point beyond Texas, [Louisiana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louisiana "Louisiana"), [Arkansas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arkansas "Arkansas"), [Oklahoma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oklahoma "Oklahoma"), [New Mexico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Mexico "New Mexico"), [Kansas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kansas "Kansas"), [Mississippi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mississippi "Mississippi"), [Alabama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alabama "Alabama"), and [Missouri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Missouri "Missouri"). However, the amendment was entirely repealed in an all-party compromise that took effect in 2014, and Love Field is now able to service any city in America.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transportation_in_Dallas#cite_note-8)

[Fort Pitt Bridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Pitt_Bridge "Fort Pitt Bridge") with [Downtown Pittsburgh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Downtown_Pittsburgh "Downtown Pittsburgh") in the background

A large metropolitan area that is surrounded by rivers and hills, [Pittsburgh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsburgh "Pittsburgh") has an infrastructure system that has been built out over the years to include roads, tunnels, bridges, railroads, inclines, bike paths, and stairways; however, the hills and rivers still form many barriers to transportation within the city.

## Roads and infrastructure

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Transportation_in_Pittsburgh&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Roads and infrastructure")]

The high number of freeze/thaw cycles during the winter is sometimes blamed for the difficulty of maintaining local roads.

### Streets

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Transportation_in_Pittsburgh&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Streets")]

[![Image 5](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/77/Pittsburgh_1795_large.jpg/250px-Pittsburgh_1795_large.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Pittsburgh_1795_large.jpg)

A 1795 map of [Pittsburgh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsburgh "Pittsburgh")

[Pittsburgh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsburgh "Pittsburgh") is home to several notable streets. [Roslyn Place](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roslyn_Place_(Street) "Roslyn Place (Street)") is a small wooden-paved [cul-de-sac](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dead_end_(street) "Dead end (street)") located in the [Shadyside](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shadyside_(Pittsburgh) "Shadyside (Pittsburgh)") neighborhood of [Pittsburgh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsburgh "Pittsburgh"), [Pennsylvania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pennsylvania "Pennsylvania"). The street was built in 1914 in the [Nicolson Pavement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicolson_pavement "Nicolson pavement") style and is home to the historic [Roslyn Place district](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roslyn_Place_(district) "Roslyn Place (district)").

[Canton Avenue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canton_Avenue "Canton Avenue") is the steepest officially recorded public street in the [United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States "United States").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transportation_in_Pittsburgh#cite_note-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transportation_in_Pittsburgh#cite_note-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transportation_in_Pittsburgh#cite_note-3)

[East Carson Street](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Side_Flats_(Pittsburgh) "South Side Flats (Pittsburgh)") has one of the largest concentrations of 19th-century homes, which has prompted outsiders to call the neighborhood the city's [Georgetown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgetown,_Washington,_D.C. "Georgetown, Washington, D.C.").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transportation_in_Pittsburgh#cite_note-4) It includes many bars and restaurants as well as residences.

[Grant Street](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grant_Street "Grant Street") is the main government and business corridor in [Pittsburgh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsburgh "Pittsburgh"), [Pennsylvania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pennsylvania "Pennsylvania"). It is home to the global headquarters of [U.S. Steel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Steel "U.S. Steel"), [Koppers Chemicals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Koppers "Koppers"), [Federated Investors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federated_Investors "Federated Investors"), and [Oxford Development](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxford_Development "Oxford Development"). It is also home to the seat of [Allegheny County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania "Allegheny County, Pennsylvania"), the City of Pittsburgh, and the regional Federal Government offices. It is part of the [Pittsburgh Central Downtown Historic District](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsburgh_Central_Downtown_Historic_District "Pittsburgh Central Downtown Historic District").

### Expressways

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Transportation_in_Pittsburgh&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Expressways")]

[![Image 7](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/05/Pittsburgh_map.PNG/250px-Pittsburgh_map.PNG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Pittsburgh_map.PNG)

Map showing major highways in Pittsburgh and its surrounding region

The main highway connecting Pittsburgh to the [Pennsylvania Turnpike](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pennsylvania_Turnpike "Pennsylvania Turnpike") ([I-76](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interstate_76_(east) "Interstate 76 (east)")) on the east is [I-376](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interstate_376 "Interstate 376"), known to locals as the "Parkway East." It includes the locally notorious Squirrel Hill interchange, where unusual traffic patterns and the adjoining [tunnel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Squirrel_Hill_Tunnel "Squirrel Hill Tunnel") often cause traffic congestion. Several accidents have involved tall trucks getting stuck against the tunnel roof. Also part of I-376 is the "Parkway West," which leads from downtown Pittsburgh to the [Pittsburgh International Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsburgh_International_Airport "Pittsburgh International Airport")'s main terminal and leads into the contiguous Airport Parkway and Southern Expressway. [I-279](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/I-279 "I-279"), known as the "Parkway North," runs north of the city to merge with [I-79](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interstate_79 "Interstate 79"). It connects the city with the North Hills and the Cranberry area. There is no "Parkway South".

[I-579](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interstate_579 "Interstate 579"), or the "Crosstown Boulevard," is a spur off of I-279 that alleviates downtown and North Shore traffic headed north or south and to events at either the [convention center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsburgh_Convention_Center "Pittsburgh Convention Center") or the [PPG Paints Arena](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PPG_Paints_Arena "PPG Paints Arena").

North of the city, the Parkway North and a short section of Interstate 579 over the [Veterans Bridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Veterans_Bridge_(Pittsburgh) "Veterans Bridge (Pittsburgh)") have reversible [high occupancy vehicle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/High-occupancy_vehicle_lane "High-occupancy vehicle lane") HOV lanes for rush-hour commuting, which require a minimum of two occupants per vehicle for use; no electric/hybrid vehicle "HOV OK" program has yet been made available. On August 25, 1995, six people were killed in a head-on collision on the HOV lanes after PennDOT employee William Dean Snyder failed to follow procedures. Snyder maintained the traffic gates open for both directions simultaneously.

Main article: [Allegheny County Belt System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Allegheny_County_Belt_System "Allegheny County Belt System")

Unlike many other major U.S. cities, Pittsburgh lacks a dedicated contiguous beltway surrounding the city. [I-76](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interstate_76_(east) "Interstate 76 (east)") ([Pennsylvania Turnpike](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pennsylvania_Turnpike "Pennsylvania Turnpike")), [I-79](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/I-79 "I-79"), and [I-70](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/I-70 "I-70") form a roughly triangular-shaped "beltway," but the distance of these roads from the city center and the need to exit and enter each leg to continue circling the city render them impractical as a beltway; commuters are forced to use secondary roads to go from suburb to suburb. The [Allegheny County Belt System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Allegheny_County_Belt_System "Allegheny County Belt System") is an attempt to address this without building additional infrastructure. The [Pittsburgh Wayfinder System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsburgh_Wayfinder_System "Pittsburgh Wayfinder System") is a similar system that aims to guide travelers to popular destinations and services in the city proper.

## Pittsburgh Regional Transit

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Transportation_in_Pittsburgh&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Pittsburgh Regional Transit")]

Main article: [Pittsburgh Regional Transit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsburgh_Regional_Transit "Pittsburgh Regional Transit")

Local public transportation is coordinated by [Pittsburgh Regional Transit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsburgh_Regional_Transit "Pittsburgh Regional Transit") (PRT), the 14th-largest urban [mass transit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mass_transit "Mass transit") system in the [United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States "United States"). It services 730 square miles (1,900 km 2), including all of [Allegheny County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania "Allegheny County, Pennsylvania") and portions of [Armstrong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Armstrong_County,_Pennsylvania "Armstrong County, Pennsylvania"), [Beaver](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beaver_County,_Pennsylvania "Beaver County, Pennsylvania"), [Washington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_County,_Pennsylvania "Washington County, Pennsylvania"), and [Westmoreland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Westmoreland_County,_Pennsylvania "Westmoreland County, Pennsylvania") counties.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transportation_in_Pittsburgh#cite_note-6) PRT maintains a network of intracity [bus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bus "Bus") routes, two [inclines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Funicular "Funicular") on Mt. Washington above Downtown (mostly a tourist attraction rather than a means of commuting), and a [light rail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rapid_transit "Rapid transit")/[busway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bus_rapid_transit "Bus rapid transit") system. The transit agency discontinued its [commuter rail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commuter_rail "Commuter rail") system, the [PATrain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PATrain "PATrain"), in 1989. However, A New Line To [Arnold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arnold,_Pennsylvania "Arnold, Pennsylvania") Has Been Proposed Since 2009.

### Light rail

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Transportation_in_Pittsburgh&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Light rail")]

A light rail vehicle departs [Station Square](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Station_Square_(PAT_station) "Station Square (PAT station)") and prepares to enter the [Mount Washington Transit Tunnel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Washington_Transit_Tunnel "Mount Washington Transit Tunnel").

The light rail network is a direct descendant of the original [streetcar system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsburgh_Railways "Pittsburgh Railways"), which once numbered dozens of lines and included [interurban](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interurban "Interurban") routes to neighboring cities such as [Washington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington,_Pennsylvania "Washington, Pennsylvania") and [Charleroi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charleroi,_Pennsylvania "Charleroi, Pennsylvania"). The current network comprises five routes on 25 miles (40 km) of track, operated by modern articulated [light rail vehicles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Light_rail_vehicles "Light rail vehicles"). However, most is on dedicated right-of-way, including the [Mt. Washington Transit Tunnel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mt._Washington_Transit_Tunnel "Mt. Washington Transit Tunnel"), trains still [street run](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Street_running "Street running") in the Beechview neighborhood. Once across the [Monongahela River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monongahela_River "Monongahela River"), trains enter a subway to serve [Downtown Pittsburgh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Downtown_Pittsburgh "Downtown Pittsburgh"). Since March 2012, the [North Shore Connector](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Shore_Connector "North Shore Connector") has extended service across the Allegheny River, via tunnel, to such destinations as [PNC Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PNC_Park "PNC Park"), [Heinz Field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heinz_Field "Heinz Field"), and [Rivers Casino](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rivers_Casino_(Pittsburgh) "Rivers Casino (Pittsburgh)").

### Busways and Bus Rapid Transit (BRT)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Transportation_in_Pittsburgh&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Busways and Bus Rapid Transit (BRT)")]

[![Image 11](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/94/Busway_%2831492662931%29.jpg/250px-Busway_%2831492662931%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Busway_(31492662931).jpg)

[Herron station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herron_station "Herron station") on the East Busway

Main articles: [Pittsburgh Regional Transit §Bus rapid transit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsburgh_Regional_Transit#Bus_rapid_transit "Pittsburgh Regional Transit"), [South Busway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Busway "South Busway"), [Martin Luther King Jr. East Busway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Luther_King_Jr._East_Busway "Martin Luther King Jr. East Busway"), and [West Busway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Busway "West Busway")

PRT operates over 800 buses on both standard routes and [bus rapid transit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bus_rapid_transit "Bus rapid transit") routes in Allegheny County. The latter use high-speed [articulated buses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Articulated_buses "Articulated buses") that run at grade and above ground on their own right-of-way with platform stations, much like a rail system. In some instances, such as the Mount Washington tunnel, these buses travel along paved sections of the light rail line. There are currently three routes: the [South Busway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Busway "South Busway"), from downtown to the southern part of Allegheny County, the [Martin Luther King Jr. East Busway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Luther_King_Jr._East_Busway "Martin Luther King Jr. East Busway"), from the [Amtrak station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsburgh_(Amtrak_station) "Pittsburgh (Amtrak station)") to the eastern suburbs, and the [West Busway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Busway "West Busway"), to the western suburbs. Plans include extending the West Busway to the [Pittsburgh International Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsburgh_International_Airport "Pittsburgh International Airport").

All light rail/busway stations outside the downtown have PRT station shuttles that serve the surrounding neighborhoods, and sections of the metropolitan area not served by the light rail/busway system, including most of the northern suburbs, have regular PRT bus routes. The mass transit systems of [Beaver](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beaver_County_Transit_Authority "Beaver County Transit Authority"), [Fayette](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fayette_Area_Coordinated_Transportation "Fayette Area Coordinated Transportation"), [Lawrence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Castle_Area_Transit_Authority "New Castle Area Transit Authority"), [Washington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_County_Transportation_Authority "Washington County Transportation Authority"), and [Westmoreland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Westmoreland_County_Transit_Authority "Westmoreland County Transit Authority") counties (including [Mid Mon Valley Transit Authority](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mid_Mon_Valley_Transit_Authority "Mid Mon Valley Transit Authority")) operate their own commuter shuttles to and from the city; the private company Myers Coach Line operates commuter service from Butler County.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transportation_in_Pittsburgh#cite_note-7) The mass transit system of [Monongalia County, West Virginia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mountain_Line_Transit_Authority "Mountain Line Transit Authority") also provides connections to Pittsburgh. In early 2005, the Southwestern Pennsylvania Commission proposed combining Pittsburgh Regional Transit, then known as Port Authority, with the nine surrounding metro counties' transit agencies.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transportation_in_Pittsburgh#cite_note-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transportation_in_Pittsburgh#cite_note-9)[_[failed verification](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Verifiability "Wikipedia:Verifiability")_]

The following colors designate busways:

*    Green—bus routes using the [West Busway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Busway "West Busway"), designated with a 'G'
*    Purple—bus routes using the [Martin Luther King Jr. East Busway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Luther_King_Jr._East_Busway "Martin Luther King Jr. East Busway"), designated with a 'P'
*    Orange—bus routes using the [I-279](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/I-279 "I-279") HOV lane, designated with an 'O'
*    Yellow—bus routes using the [South Busway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Busway "South Busway"), designated with a 'Y'

On July 22, 2011, the Port Authority approved spending at least $1 million, including $837,993 in federal funding and $209,498 in county money, to study developing a rapid bus line from downtown to the Oakland section. The study was projected to take 18 months and use no money from Pittsburgh Regional Transit's operating budget. The study resulted in planning for the new **University Line**. Rerouting existing bus routes and implementing other system changes began in October 2023.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transportation_in_Pittsburgh#cite_note-10) The first phase of construction began in Downtown Pittsburgh on September 13, 2023, and was completed in Summer 2025.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transportation_in_Pittsburgh#cite_note-:0-11)The second phase of construction started in Uptown and Oakland in January 2025 and is expected to be completed in 2027.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transportation_in_Pittsburgh#cite_note-:0-11)

## Pedestrians and bicycling

### Pedestrian staircases

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Transportation_in_Pittsburgh&action=edit&section=15 "Edit section: Pedestrian staircases")]

Main article: [Steps of Pittsburgh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steps_of_Pittsburgh "Steps of Pittsburgh")

[![Image 16](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/23/Duquense_University_steps_%2811617009%29.jpg/250px-Duquense_University_steps_%2811617009%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Duquense_University_steps_(11617009).jpg)

Public staircase at [Duquesne University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duquesne_University "Duquesne University").

Pittsburgh has more public staircases (737) than any other city in the United States, followed by [Cincinnati](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cincinnati "Cincinnati") and [San Francisco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Francisco "San Francisco").[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transportation_in_Pittsburgh#cite_note-15) Many of these staircases have [street names](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Street_name "Street name"), and lead to hillside neighborhoods that can be difficult to access by car in winter.

The large number of steps is an engineering approach to the topography upon which the City of Pittsburgh is built. According to author Martin Aurand, Pittsburgh "lies unevenly on unruly land". The city is located at the confluence of two rivers which cut through elevated land of the [Appalachian Plateau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Appalachian_Plateau "Appalachian Plateau"). The city is settled at elevations ranging from 710 to 1,300 feet (220 to 400 m) above sea level.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transportation_in_Pittsburgh#cite_note-16)

### Pedestrian trails

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Transportation_in_Pittsburgh&action=edit&section=16 "Edit section: Pedestrian trails")]

[![Image 17](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b7/Strip_District_21st_St_trail_jeh.jpg/250px-Strip_District_21st_St_trail_jeh.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Strip_District_21st_St_trail_jeh.jpg)

Unpaved portion of the [Three Rivers Heritage Trail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Three_Rivers_Heritage_Trail "Three Rivers Heritage Trail") in Strip District

Pittsburgh has a thriving cycling community despite steep hills and variable weather. Efforts have been made to incorporate the bicycle into the transportation system. The [Three Rivers Heritage Trail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Three_Rivers_Heritage_Trail "Three Rivers Heritage Trail") encompasses all the trails in the city. The Eliza Furnace Trail, known locally as the "Jail Trail", stretches from downtown (at the Allegheny County Jail) to the East End region, where trail access can be found along some roads. The North Shore Trail spans from the [Alcosan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcosan "Alcosan") plant along the Ohio River and continues along the Allegheny River to Millvale. The Southside Trail follows the Monongahela River and, beyond Baldwin Borough, connects to McKeesport via the [Great Allegheny Passage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Allegheny_Passage "Great Allegheny Passage"). This trail, in connection with the [C&O Canal Trail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chesapeake_and_Ohio_Canal_National_Historical_Park "Chesapeake and Ohio Canal National Historical Park"), forms a continuous motorist-free route from [Point State Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Point_State_Park "Point State Park") in Pittsburgh to [Washington, D.C.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington,_D.C. "Washington, D.C.") PAT has installed bike racks on all buses. It allows bikes on its subway/busway system at all times.

### Bicycles

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Transportation_in_Pittsburgh&action=edit&section=17 "Edit section: Bicycles")]

[![Image 18](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a7/Healthy_Ride_station_in_Pittsburgh_01.JPG/250px-Healthy_Ride_station_in_Pittsburgh_01.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Healthy_Ride_station_in_Pittsburgh_01.JPG)

[Healthy Ride](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Healthy_Ride "Healthy Ride") station

Bike Pittsburgh (BikePGH) is the local bicycle advocacy group and is working to make Pittsburgh increasingly safe, accessible, and friendly to bicycle transportation.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] The non-profit bike collective, Free Ride,[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transportation_in_Pittsburgh#cite_note-17)[_[non-primary source needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:No\_original\_research#Primary,\_secondary\_and\_tertiary\_sources "Wikipedia:No original research")_] recycles bicycles and bike parts, teaches bicycle construction, and has programs to sell or earn a rebuilt bicycle. Additionally, bicycles can be borrowed at two places along the Heritage Trail through the Friends of the Riverfront/Dasani Blue Bikes program.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

In 2014, the city began installing segregated bike lanes, which provide greater physical safety for bikers.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transportation_in_Pittsburgh#cite_note-18) On September 6, bike lanes that stretch from Downtown Pittsburgh to the 16th Street Bridge on Penn Avenue were installed. To accommodate these bike lanes, the Westbound lane of Penn Avenue was removed, making it one-way. Other segregated bike lanes were installed on Schenley Drive in Oakland, and Saline Street in Greenfield.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transportation_in_Pittsburgh#cite_note-19)

The "[Healthy Ride](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Healthy_Ride "Healthy Ride")" [bicycle-sharing system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bicycle-sharing_system "Bicycle-sharing system") entered service in Spring 2016, supplied by [Nextbike](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nextbike "Nextbike"). The price was $2 per half-hour, or $12 or $20 per month.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transportation_in_Pittsburgh#cite_note-20) In 2022, the system went through a full rebrand and is now known as POGOH. The equipment and software are acquired through PBSC, an industry leader in [bikeshare](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bicycle-sharing_system "Bicycle-sharing system").

## Freight Railroads

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Transportation_in_Pittsburgh&action=edit&section=18 "Edit section: Freight Railroads")]

[![Image 19](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/22/CSX_train_crossing_under_the_Smithfield_Bridge_in_Pittsburgh_%289382313814%29.jpg/250px-CSX_train_crossing_under_the_Smithfield_Bridge_in_Pittsburgh_%289382313814%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:CSX_train_crossing_under_the_Smithfield_Bridge_in_Pittsburgh_(9382313814).jpg)

CSX train crossing under the Smithfield Bridge in Pittsburgh

During the heyday of the steel industry, Pittsburgh was among the largest rail centers not only in the nation, but the world. For many years, the multiple rail crossings in the suburb of [Port Perry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Port_Perry,_Pennsylvania "Port Perry, Pennsylvania") at the mouth of [Turtle Creek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turtle_Creek_(Monongahela_River) "Turtle Creek (Monongahela River)") on the [Monongahela River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monongahela_River "Monongahela River") and adjacent to the [Edgar Thomson Works](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edgar_Thomson_Works "Edgar Thomson Works") and [Duquesne mills](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duquesne,_Pennsylvania "Duquesne, Pennsylvania"), was the highest concentration of freight traffic in the world. Even today, with river traffic included, Port Perry is often very near or at the top of the list. The [Conway Yard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conway_Yard "Conway Yard") to the west of the city along the [Ohio River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ohio_River "Ohio River") was the largest rail yard in the world from 1956 until 1980. From the beginning of the industrial era in America through its collapse in the 1980s, Pittsburgh was a key market for the nation's largest and most important railroads (most notably the [Pennsylvania Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pennsylvania_Railroad "Pennsylvania Railroad") [the largest company in the world for much of the 20th century], and the [New York Central Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_Central_Railroad "New York Central Railroad") [via the [Pittsburgh & Lake Erie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsburgh_and_Lake_Erie_Railroad "Pittsburgh and Lake Erie Railroad")], [Baltimore and Ohio Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baltimore_and_Ohio_Railroad "Baltimore and Ohio Railroad") and [Pittsburgh & West Virginia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsburgh_and_West_Virginia_Railway "Pittsburgh and West Virginia Railway")). Despite the near-complete collapse of heavy industry in the Northeast, Pittsburgh remains an extremely important link in the nation's rail network. Current railroads in Pittsburgh include:

### Class I railroads

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Transportation_in_Pittsburgh&action=edit&section=19 "Edit section: Class I railroads")]

#### Norfolk Southern (NS)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Transportation_in_Pittsburgh&action=edit&section=20 "Edit section: Norfolk Southern (NS)")]

[Norfolk Southern](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norfolk_Southern "Norfolk Southern") operates the former assets of [Conrail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conrail "Conrail"), composed of the [Pennsylvania Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pennsylvania_Railroad "Pennsylvania Railroad"), instrumental in the formation of modern Pittsburgh. NS operates three lines through Pittsburgh:

*   the original line, the [Pittsburgh Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsburgh_Line "Pittsburgh Line"), from U.S. Steel's [Edgar Thomson Steel Mill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edgar_Thomson_Works "Edgar Thomson Works") in Braddock, PA, over the Allegheny River near Downtown Pittsburgh, into Island Ave Yard where it becomes the [Fort Wayne Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Wayne_Line "Fort Wayne Line");
*   the [Mon Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mon_Line "Mon Line"), along the south bank of the Monongahela River from [West Brownsville, PA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Brownsville,_PA "West Brownsville, PA"), to Island Ave Yard, formerly the Pittsburgh, Virginia and Charleston Railroad. This line is used by coal trains from southern Pennsylvania and trains with [over-height cars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Double-stack_rail_transport "Double-stack rail transport") that cannot fit under the roof of Penn Station on the Pittsburgh Line, accessing it via a branch just east of Braddock to the [Port Perry bridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PRR_Port_Perry_Bridge "PRR Port Perry Bridge"). The Mon Line joins the Fort Wayne Line at Island Ave Yard after crossing the Ohio River on the [Ohio Connecting (OC) Railroad bridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ohio_Connecting_Railroad_Bridge "Ohio Connecting Railroad Bridge");
*   the [Conemaugh Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conemaugh_Line "Conemaugh Line"), along the north shore of the Allegheny River, serving several coal branch lines and power plants. Operations are centered on a small yard in [Etna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Etna,_Pennsylvania "Etna, Pennsylvania"), PA.

On the Mon and Pittsburgh lines, over 60 trains a day pass through the city.

#### CSX

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Transportation_in_Pittsburgh&action=edit&section=21 "Edit section: CSX")]

[CSX](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CSX "CSX") operates the former [Baltimore and Ohio Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baltimore_and_Ohio_Railroad "Baltimore and Ohio Railroad") (B&O) and the [Pittsburgh and Lake Erie Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsburgh_and_Lake_Erie_Railroad "Pittsburgh and Lake Erie Railroad") (P&LE). Many of the old B&O lines have been removed or are unused. Formerly an important part of the B&O system, Glenwood Yard is leased and operated by the Allegheny Valley Railroad for local jobs. The yard used to give access to the B&O's [Grant Street Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grant_Street_Station "Grant Street Station") in Downtown Pittsburgh. The building has been rebuilt into a PNC Bank building, and the old right-of-way is now a bike [path](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eliza_Furnace_Trail "Eliza Furnace Trail"). The B&O main line, which runs north and under Pittsburgh via the [Schenley Tunnel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schenley_Tunnel "Schenley Tunnel"), is now used by the AVR. The [33rd Street Railroad Bridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/33rd_Street_Railroad_Bridge "33rd Street Railroad Bridge") over the Allegheny River is still used: AVR trains connect with Norfolk Southern's Pittsburgh Line about a mile east of Penn Station. CSX freight trains use the former P&LE through [McKeesport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/McKeesport,_Pennsylvania "McKeesport, Pennsylvania"), PA, and [Braddock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Braddock,_Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania "Braddock, Allegheny County, Pennsylvania"), PA, before crossing the Mononghela River into [Homestead](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homestead,_Pennsylvania "Homestead, Pennsylvania"), PA. The P&LE line and the Mon Line run side by side until the Mon Line crosses the Ohio Connecting Railroad Bridge at [McKees Rocks, Pennsylvania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/McKees_Rocks,_Pennsylvania "McKees Rocks, Pennsylvania"). On an average day, the P&LE line carries about 30–35 trains.

### Class II railroads

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Transportation_in_Pittsburgh&action=edit&section=22 "Edit section: Class II railroads")]

The [Wheeling & Lake Erie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wheeling_and_Lake_Erie_Railway_(1990) "Wheeling and Lake Erie Railway (1990)") is a regional railroad incorporated in 1990 after the [Norfolk and Western Railway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norfolk_and_Western_Railway "Norfolk and Western Railway") sold trackage from the original [Wheeling & Lake Erie Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wheeling_and_Lake_Erie_Railway_(1916%E2%80%931988) "Wheeling and Lake Erie Railway (1916–1988)").

The W&LE is the largest Ohio-based railroad and among the largest regional railroads in the country, with a service area that includes 840 miles of track in Ohio, West Virginia, Pennsylvania, and Maryland.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transportation_in_Pittsburgh#cite_note-21)

#### Bessemer & Lake Erie

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Transportation_in_Pittsburgh&action=edit&section=23 "Edit section: Bessemer & Lake Erie")]

The [Bessemer & Lake Erie Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bessemer_&_Lake_Erie_Railroad "Bessemer & Lake Erie Railroad") runs north from the North Bessemer Yard in [Penn Hills](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Penn_Hills_Township,_Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania "Penn Hills Township, Allegheny County, Pennsylvania") to [Conneaut, Ohio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conneaut,_Ohio "Conneaut, Ohio"). In 2004, the B&LE was purchased by [Canadian National Railway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadian_National_Railway "Canadian National Railway").

### Class III railroads

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Transportation_in_Pittsburgh&action=edit&section=24 "Edit section: Class III railroads")]

#### Allegheny Valley Railroad

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Transportation_in_Pittsburgh&action=edit&section=25 "Edit section: Allegheny Valley Railroad")]

The [Allegheny Valley Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Allegheny_Valley_Railroad_(1995) "Allegheny Valley Railroad (1995)") runs mostly on former [Pennsylvania Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pennsylvania_Railroad "Pennsylvania Railroad") and [Baltimore and Ohio Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baltimore_and_Ohio_Railroad "Baltimore and Ohio Railroad") lines.

#### Pittsburgh and Ohio Central Railroad

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Transportation_in_Pittsburgh&action=edit&section=26 "Edit section: Pittsburgh and Ohio Central Railroad")]

The [Pittsburgh and Ohio Central Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsburgh_and_Ohio_Central_Railroad "Pittsburgh and Ohio Central Railroad") operates former [Pennsylvania Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pennsylvania_Railroad "Pennsylvania Railroad") trackage on the [Chartiers Branch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chartiers_Branch "Chartiers Branch") and the [Panhandle Route](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Panhandle_Route "Panhandle Route") to the southwest.

#### Union Railroad

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Transportation_in_Pittsburgh&action=edit&section=27 "Edit section: Union Railroad")]

[Union Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Union_Railroad_(Pittsburgh,_Pennsylvania) "Union Railroad (Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania)") mainly serves the last remaining steel mills in the city. It has interchanges with the B&LE at North Bessemer.
