### Platforms and tracks

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Grand_Central_Madison&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Platforms and tracks")]

[![Image 106](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/5f/GCM_%2852605456333%29.jpg/250px-GCM_%2852605456333%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:GCM_(52605456333).jpg)

Lower-level platforms viewed from the mezzanine

LIRR trains arrive and depart from the twin station caverns and through a tunnel located 140 ft (43 m) below [Park Avenue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Park_Avenue_(Manhattan) "Park Avenue (Manhattan)") and more than 90 ft (27 m) below the Metro-North tracks.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Central_Madison#cite_note-ESA-FEIS-73)[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Central_Madison#cite_note-wsj-2012-04-262-64)[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Central_Madison#cite_note-75)

The LIRR terminal contains four platforms and eight tracks (numbered 201–204 and 301–304) in two bi-level caverns.[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Central_Madison#cite_note-76) There are four tracks and two platforms in each of the two caverns, with each cavern containing two tracks on one island platform per level.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Central_Madison#cite_note-Dobnik2015-65)[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Central_Madison#cite_note-LIHerald20180821-72)

### Exits

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Grand_Central_Madison&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Exits")]

The MTA originally planned to build and open entrances at 44th, 45th, 47th, and 48th Streets.[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Central_Madison#cite_note-MTA-ESA-EIS-Mod-AppendixB-2006-77):3[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Central_Madison#cite_note-Ocean_2015-69)[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Central_Madison#cite_note-MTA-EntranceMemo-2018-78):5 The station connects to existing entrances at [Grand Central North](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Central_Terminal#Grand_Central_North "Grand Central Terminal"). The new LIRR station also contains entrances at 335 Madison Avenue, near the southeast corner with 44th Street; at [270 Park Avenue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/270_Park_Avenue_(2021%E2%80%93present) "270 Park Avenue (2021–present)") and 280 Park Avenue near 47th and 48th–49th Streets, respectively; and at 347 Madison Avenue, on the east side of the avenue at 45th Street. An entrance on 46th Street between Lexington and Park Avenue was also built, connecting with Grand Central North.[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Central_Madison#cite_note-MTA-EntranceMemo-2018-78):5–6 However, the MTA later announced its intent to defer construction of an entrance at 48th Street because the owner of 415 Madison Avenue wanted to undertake a major construction project on the site.[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Central_Madison#cite_note-MTA-EntranceMemo-2018-78):7 The MTA also connected the new station to the existing 47th Street cross-passage.[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Central_Madison#cite_note-MTA-ESA-EIS-Mod-AppendixB-2006-77):3[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Central_Madison#cite_note-Ocean_2015-69)

Another entrance with an elevator, a stair, and two staircases was developed at 45th Street.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Central_Madison#cite_note-Castillo_e881-48) This entrance opened in 2026 and is part of the proposed [343 Madison Avenue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/343_Madison_Avenue "343 Madison Avenue") development.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Central_Madison#cite_note-Castillo_z041-60)[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Central_Madison#cite_note-Stark-Miller_v405-61) Two entrances north of 47th Street are being planned as well.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Central_Madison#cite_note-Heyward_v735-47)

## Art

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Grand_Central_Madison&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Art")]

[![Image 107](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/17/GCM_%2852605203234%29.jpg/250px-GCM_%2852605203234%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:GCM_(52605203234).jpg)

_The Presence_, a [Kiki Smith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kiki_Smith "Kiki Smith") mosaic

Like the [art in the original Grand Central Terminal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Central_Terminal_art "Grand Central Terminal art"), the new station includes permanent [site-specific works of art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Site-specific_art "Site-specific art"). Among them are five large glass [mosaics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mosaic "Mosaic") on natural themes by [Kiki Smith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kiki_Smith "Kiki Smith"). The Madison Concourse level contains _River Light_, an 80 ft-long (24 m) abstract, largely blue-and-white depiction of sunshine on the [East River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_River "East River").[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Central_Madison#cite_note-:0-79) The other four, one level down in the LIRR mezzanine, are: _The Presence_, a landscape with a deer; _The Sound_, a seascape with a gull; _The Spring_, featuring four turkeys; and _The Water's Way_, a beach scene. "I wanted places for people to say, 'Meet you by the deer'," Smith told _The New York Times_.[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Central_Madison#cite_note-:0-79)

The Madison Concourse level also holds an even larger 120 ft-long (37 m) mosaic by [Yayoi Kusama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yayoi_Kusama "Yayoi Kusama"): _A Message of Love, Directly from My Heart unto the Universe_.[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Central_Madison#cite_note-:0-79)

**Grand Central Madison**, also known as the **Madison Concourse** and announced on trains as **Grand Central**, is a [commuter rail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commuter_rail "Commuter rail") terminal for the [Long Island Rail Road (LIRR)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Long_Island_Rail_Road "Long Island Rail Road") in the [Midtown East](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Midtown_East,_Manhattan "Midtown East, Manhattan") neighborhood of [Manhattan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manhattan "Manhattan"), in [New York City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City "New York City"). It sits beneath [Grand Central Terminal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Central_Terminal "Grand Central Terminal"), which serves the [Metro-North Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metro-North_Railroad "Metro-North Railroad") – the other commuter rail system operated by the [Metropolitan Transportation Authority (MTA)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metropolitan_Transportation_Authority "Metropolitan Transportation Authority").[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Central_Madison#cite_note-7) Built as part of the [East Side Access](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Side_Access "East Side Access") project, the terminal's construction commenced in 2008, and it opened on January 25, 2023.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Central_Madison#cite_note-125Opening-5)

Grand Central Madison was built to reduce travel times to and from Manhattan's [East Side](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Side_(Manhattan) "East Side (Manhattan)") and to ease congestion at [Penn Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pennsylvania_Station_(New_York_City) "Pennsylvania Station (New York City)"), the [West Side](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Side_(Manhattan) "West Side (Manhattan)") station where all Manhattan-bound LIRR trains had terminated since 1910. The new terminal enables passengers to transfer to Metro-North's [Harlem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harlem_Line "Harlem Line"), [Hudson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson_Line_(Metro-North) "Hudson Line (Metro-North)"), and [New Haven Lines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Haven_Line "New Haven Line"), as well as the [New York City Subway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City_Subway "New York City Subway") at [Grand Central–42nd Street station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Central%E2%80%9342nd_Street_station "Grand Central–42nd Street station").

The station is managed by **MTA Grand Central Madison Operating Company** (GCMOC), a [subsidiary public benefit corporation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_state_public-benefit_corporations "New York state public-benefit corporations") of the MTA created in October 2021 to manage the assets of the East Side Access project.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Central_Madison#cite_note-subsidiary-8) The company is led by Paul Grether and has five total employees, with most services being handled by centralized functions at the MTA.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Central_Madison#cite_note-subsidiary-8)

## Services

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Grand_Central_Madison&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Services")]

[![Image 19](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/03/Inaugural_Train_Ride_To_Grand_Central_Madison_-_52649236475.jpg/250px-Inaugural_Train_Ride_To_Grand_Central_Madison_-_52649236475.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Inaugural_Train_Ride_To_Grand_Central_Madison_-_52649236475.jpg)

A LIRR train of [M9 cars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M9_(railcar) "M9 (railcar)") on Track 303

The station serves the [Long Island Rail Road](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Long_Island_Rail_Road "Long Island Rail Road")'s [Main Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Main_Line_(Long_Island_Rail_Road) "Main Line (Long Island Rail Road)"),[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Central_Madison#cite_note-9) which connects to all passenger branches and almost all stations.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Central_Madison#cite_note-10) Service started on January 25, 2023, with a shuttle to [Jamaica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jamaica_station "Jamaica station").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Central_Madison#cite_note-125Opening-5) Full service at the station began on February 27, 2023, with trains continuing beyond Jamaica to most branches.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Central_Madison#cite_note-11)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Central_Madison#cite_note-12)

Passengers traveling to and from non-electrified portions of the LIRR system – specifically the [Oyster Bay Branch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oyster_Bay_Branch "Oyster Bay Branch"), the [Port Jefferson Branch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Port_Jefferson_Branch "Port Jefferson Branch") east of [Huntington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Huntington_station_(LIRR) "Huntington station (LIRR)"), the [Main Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Main_Line_(Long_Island_Rail_Road) "Main Line (Long Island Rail Road)") east of [Ronkonkoma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ronkonkoma_station "Ronkonkoma station"), and the [Montauk Branch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montauk_Branch "Montauk Branch") east of [Babylon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Babylon_station "Babylon station") – must transfer between trains at Jamaica or points east therefrom, as the [bilevel C3 coaches](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C3_(railcar) "C3 (railcar)") used in non-electrified areas cannot fit through the [63rd Street Tunnel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/63rd_Street_Tunnel "63rd Street Tunnel").[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Central_Madison#cite_note-13)

Grand Central Madison also provides an alternative route from the east side of Manhattan and from Metro-North lines to [John F. Kennedy International Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_F._Kennedy_International_Airport "John F. Kennedy International Airport"), via a connection with the [AirTrain JFK](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AirTrain_JFK "AirTrain JFK") people mover at [Jamaica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jamaica_station "Jamaica station").[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Central_Madison#cite_note-14)

### Planning and construction

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Grand_Central_Madison&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Planning and construction")]

[![Image 20](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/77/ESA_Progress_Photos_-_Concourse_and_Terminal.jpg/250px-ESA_Progress_Photos_-_Concourse_and_Terminal.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:ESA_Progress_Photos_-_Concourse_and_Terminal.jpg)

LIRR concourse construction in 2019

Formal proposals to bring Long Island Rail Road trains to the east side of Manhattan date to 1963.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Central_Madison#cite_note-15) In 1968, the [63rd Street Tunnel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/63rd_Street_Tunnel "63rd Street Tunnel") and a LIRR "Metropolitan Transportation Center" at [48th Street](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/48th_Street_(Manhattan) "48th Street (Manhattan)") and [Third Avenue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Avenue "Third Avenue") were proposed as part of the [Program for Action](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Program_for_Action "Program for Action").[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Central_Madison#cite_note-16) After people living near the proposed transportation center objected, the MTA's board of directors voted to instead route LIRR trains to [Grand Central](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Central_Terminal "Grand Central Terminal") by 1977.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Central_Madison#cite_note-17) However, the LIRR project was postponed indefinitely – along with several others proposed by the agency – during (and as a result of) the [1975 New York City fiscal crisis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1975_New_York_City_fiscal_crisis "1975 New York City fiscal crisis").[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Central_Madison#cite_note-18)

The East Side Access project was restarted after a study in the 1990s showed that more than half of LIRR riders work closer to Grand Central than to Penn Station.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Central_Madison#cite_note-19) The cost of the project, estimated at $4.4 billion in 2004, jumped to $6.4 billion in 2006[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Central_Madison#cite_note-20) and to $11.1 billion by 2017.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Central_Madison#cite_note-21)[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Central_Madison#cite_note-22)

In May 2022, the MTA announced that the station would be named Grand Central Madison[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Central_Madison#cite_note-23)[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Central_Madison#cite_note-24)[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Central_Madison#cite_note-25) because it sits under Grand Central Terminal and the "[Madison Avenue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Madison_Avenue "Madison Avenue") corridor".[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Central_Madison#cite_note-26)

### Opening and early years

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Grand_Central_Madison&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Opening and early years")]

The LIRR received operational control of Grand Central Madison on December 9, 2022, upon which the station and tracks became subject to [Federal Railroad Administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Railroad_Administration "Federal Railroad Administration") regulations.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Central_Madison#cite_note-27)[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Central_Madison#cite_note-28) A few weeks later, the MTA postponed the station's planned December 2022 opening because of a single ventilation fan that could not exhaust enough air.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Central_Madison#cite_note-29)[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Central_Madison#cite_note-30)[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Central_Madison#cite_note-31)[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Central_Madison#cite_note-32) On January 23, 2023, officials said the station would open and revenue service would begin on January 25.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Central_Madison#cite_note-33)[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Central_Madison#cite_note-34)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Central_Madison#cite_note-125Opening-5) The initial service was provided by the _[Grand Central Direct](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Long\_Island\_Rail\_Road#Named\_trains "Long Island Rail Road")_ – a temporary shuttle service running to and from [Jamaica station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jamaica_station "Jamaica station"), with some trains running express and others making intermediate stops at [Woodside](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Woodside_station_(LIRR) "Woodside station (LIRR)"), [Forest Hills](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forest_Hills_station_(LIRR) "Forest Hills station (LIRR)"), and [Kew Gardens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kew_Gardens_station_(LIRR) "Kew Gardens station (LIRR)").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Central_Madison#cite_note-125Opening-5) The MTA announced on February 8 that it would begin full service on February 27.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Central_Madison#cite_note-35) The Biltmore Connection to Grand Central Terminal's Biltmore Room opened in May 2023.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Central_Madison#cite_note-36) The MTA upgraded cellular service within the Grand Central Madison station and surrounding tunnels in late 2023.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Central_Madison#cite_note-37)[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Central_Madison#cite_note-38)

In early 2024, the MTA board voted to buy a battery-powered locomotive to serve as a "rescue locomotive" that could tow disabled passenger trains through the [63rd Street Tunnel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/63rd_Street_Tunnel "63rd Street Tunnel").[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Central_Madison#cite_note-39) The line had lacked one because the LIRR's locomotives could only fit through the larger [East River Tunnels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_River_Tunnels "East River Tunnels").[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Central_Madison#cite_note-40) In March 2024, Tracks Raw Bar and Grill became the first commercial tenant to sign a lease at Grand Central Madison.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Central_Madison#cite_note-41) The following month, the MTA issued a formal [request for proposals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Request_for_proposal "Request for proposal") for the station's retail space.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Central_Madison#cite_note-ABC7_New_York_2024_p171-42)[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Central_Madison#cite_note-43) The station was to have separate dining and retail areas.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Central_Madison#cite_note-ABC7_New_York_2024_p171-42) Parts of the station remained incomplete a year and a half after the station opened.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Central_Madison#cite_note-44)[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Central_Madison#cite_note-Spivack_2024_p653-45) The MTA began looking for a contractor to finish the last portions of the station that August at a cost of up to $50 million.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Central_Madison#cite_note-Spivack_2024_p653-45) In October, MTA and developer [BXP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston_Properties "Boston Properties") began building a new entrance from the intersection of 45th Street and Madison Avenue, where BXP was erecting [343 Madison Avenue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/343_Madison_Avenue "343 Madison Avenue").[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Central_Madison#cite_note-46)[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Central_Madison#cite_note-Heyward_v735-47) At the time, the entrance was planned to be completed in 2026.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Central_Madison#cite_note-Castillo_e881-48)[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Central_Madison#cite_note-49) A waiting area also opened at the station in late 2024, near the 47th Street entrance.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Central_Madison#cite_note-50) In December, [UNESCO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UNESCO "UNESCO") gave its 2024 Prix Versailles Interior Award to Grand Central Madison, calling the station one of the world's most beautiful.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Central_Madison#cite_note-51) At the end of 2024, the storefronts at Grand Central Madison remained vacant, and Tracks Raw Bar and Grill had not yet opened.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Central_Madison#cite_note-52)

The MTA announced in February 2025 that it was no longer looking for a master tenant to take over the retail space at Grand Central Madison, since most of the station's retail space had been leased out.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Central_Madison#cite_note-53) Stores are not scheduled to open until 2026 because of problems with the ventilation system.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Central_Madison#cite_note-54)[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Central_Madison#cite_note-55) The Tracks Bar opened in June 2025 as the station's first concessionaire.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Central_Madison#cite_note-56) The MTA added more benches to the mezzanine in August 2025;[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Central_Madison#cite_note-57)[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Central_Madison#cite_note-58) the benches have seat dividers to prevent people from lying on them.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Central_Madison#cite_note-59) The 343 Madison Avenue entrance opened in May 2026.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Central_Madison#cite_note-Castillo_z041-60)[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Central_Madison#cite_note-Stark-Miller_v405-61)

Grand Central Madison has an area of 700,000 sq ft (65,000 m 2), including 120,000 sq ft (11,000 m 2) for passengers and 25,000 sq ft (2,300 m 2) of retail space.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Central_Madison#cite_note-62)[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Central_Madison#cite_note-63) The station also has a total of 47 escalators—more than in the remainder of the LIRR network combined – and 22 elevators.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Central_Madison#cite_note-wsj-2012-04-262-64)

### Concourse

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Grand_Central_Madison&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Concourse")]

The retail and dining concourse, called the Madison Concourse, is reached from street level or the Metro-North terminal via stairwells and elevators.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Central_Madison#cite_note-Dobnik2015-65) It sits at the same depth as the western part of Metro-North's Lower Level, underneath tracks 38 to 42 of Metro-North's Upper Level and [Vanderbilt Avenue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vanderbilt_Avenue "Vanderbilt Avenue").[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Central_Madison#cite_note-irum-66) The concourse contains a ticket office, ticketed waiting area, nursing room, and customer-service office under 47th Street. It also has restrooms, ticket machines, and retail spaces throughout the concourse.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Central_Madison#cite_note-mta_guide-67) The only seating in the terminal is in the ticketed waiting area, which contains 29 seats; passengers can be fined $50 if they stay in the waiting area for more than 90 minutes. An MTA spokesperson said the rule was an extension of an existing restriction at Grand Central Terminal and that "a customer should not have to wait more than 90 minutes to catch their train, barring a significant service disruption".[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Central_Madison#cite_note-68)

The LIRR terminal has entrances from Grand Central Terminal's Dining Concourse and Biltmore Room, and the MTA added new entrances to the LIRR station at 45th, 46th, and 48th streets.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Central_Madison#cite_note-Ocean_2015-69)[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Central_Madison#cite_note-70) In 2021, the 45th Street entrance alone was projected to serve 10,000 passengers per day.[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Central_Madison#cite_note-WSHU_2021-71)

### Mezzanine

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Grand_Central_Madison&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Mezzanine")]

A mezzanine sits on a center level between the LIRR's two track levels.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Central_Madison#cite_note-Dobnik2015-65)[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Central_Madison#cite_note-LIHerald20180821-72) It is more than 140 ft (43 m) deep below [Park Avenue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Park_Avenue_(Manhattan) "Park Avenue (Manhattan)"),[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Central_Madison#cite_note-irum-66) and is connected to the Concourse via four banks of escalators up to 180 ft (55 m) long and descend more than 90 ft (27 m) under 45th, 46th, 47th, and 48th Streets,[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Central_Madison#cite_note-mta_guide-67)[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Central_Madison#cite_note-WSHU_2021-71) in which one of its largest has more than five escalators.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Central_Madison#cite_note-ESA-FEIS-73) One of these escalators is also the longest escalator in the city.[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Central_Madison#cite_note-74) The escalators and elevators are among the few which are privately operated in the entire MTA system.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Central_Madison#cite_note-wsj-2012-04-262-64) Additionally, the tiling around the sets of escalators and lights in the mezzanine near each set of escalators exhibits a degree of color coordination, with the set under 45th Street's lighting and tiling in shades of [light green](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Light_green "Light green"), 46th Street's in shades of [blue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue "Blue"), 47th Street's in shades of [purple](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Purple "Purple") and 48th Street's in shades of [cyan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cyan "Cyan").

### Platforms and tracks

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Grand_Central_Madison&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Platforms and tracks")]

[![Image 106](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/5f/GCM_%2852605456333%29.jpg/250px-GCM_%2852605456333%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:GCM_(52605456333).jpg)

Lower-level platforms viewed from the mezzanine

LIRR trains arrive and depart from the twin station caverns and through a tunnel located 140 ft (43 m) below [Park Avenue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Park_Avenue_(Manhattan) "Park Avenue (Manhattan)") and more than 90 ft (27 m) below the Metro-North tracks.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Central_Madison#cite_note-ESA-FEIS-73)[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Central_Madison#cite_note-wsj-2012-04-262-64)[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Central_Madison#cite_note-75)

The LIRR terminal contains four platforms and eight tracks (numbered 201–204 and 301–304) in two bi-level caverns.[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Central_Madison#cite_note-76) There are four tracks and two platforms in each of the two caverns, with each cavern containing two tracks on one island platform per level.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Central_Madison#cite_note-Dobnik2015-65)[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Central_Madison#cite_note-LIHerald20180821-72)

### Exits

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Grand_Central_Madison&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Exits")]

The MTA originally planned to build and open entrances at 44th, 45th, 47th, and 48th Streets.[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Central_Madison#cite_note-MTA-ESA-EIS-Mod-AppendixB-2006-77):3[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Central_Madison#cite_note-Ocean_2015-69)[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Central_Madison#cite_note-MTA-EntranceMemo-2018-78):5 The station connects to existing entrances at [Grand Central North](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Central_Terminal#Grand_Central_North "Grand Central Terminal"). The new LIRR station also contains entrances at 335 Madison Avenue, near the southeast corner with 44th Street; at [270 Park Avenue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/270_Park_Avenue_(2021%E2%80%93present) "270 Park Avenue (2021–present)") and 280 Park Avenue near 47th and 48th–49th Streets, respectively; and at 347 Madison Avenue, on the east side of the avenue at 45th Street. An entrance on 46th Street between Lexington and Park Avenue was also built, connecting with Grand Central North.[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Central_Madison#cite_note-MTA-EntranceMemo-2018-78):5–6 However, the MTA later announced its intent to defer construction of an entrance at 48th Street because the owner of 415 Madison Avenue wanted to undertake a major construction project on the site.[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Central_Madison#cite_note-MTA-EntranceMemo-2018-78):7 The MTA also connected the new station to the existing 47th Street cross-passage.[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Central_Madison#cite_note-MTA-ESA-EIS-Mod-AppendixB-2006-77):3[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Central_Madison#cite_note-Ocean_2015-69)

Another entrance with an elevator, a stair, and two staircases was developed at 45th Street.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Central_Madison#cite_note-Castillo_e881-48) This entrance opened in 2026 and is part of the proposed [343 Madison Avenue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/343_Madison_Avenue "343 Madison Avenue") development.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Central_Madison#cite_note-Castillo_z041-60)[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Central_Madison#cite_note-Stark-Miller_v405-61) Two entrances north of 47th Street are being planned as well.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Central_Madison#cite_note-Heyward_v735-47)

## Art

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Grand_Central_Madison&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Art")]

[![Image 107](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/17/GCM_%2852605203234%29.jpg/250px-GCM_%2852605203234%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:GCM_(52605203234).jpg)

_The Presence_, a [Kiki Smith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kiki_Smith "Kiki Smith") mosaic

Like the [art in the original Grand Central Terminal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Central_Terminal_art "Grand Central Terminal art"), the new station includes permanent [site-specific works of art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Site-specific_art "Site-specific art"). Among them are five large glass [mosaics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mosaic "Mosaic") on natural themes by [Kiki Smith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kiki_Smith "Kiki Smith"). The Madison Concourse level contains _River Light_, an 80 ft-long (24 m) abstract, largely blue-and-white depiction of sunshine on the [East River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_River "East River").[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Central_Madison#cite_note-:0-79) The other four, one level down in the LIRR mezzanine, are: _The Presence_, a landscape with a deer; _The Sound_, a seascape with a gull; _The Spring_, featuring four turkeys; and _The Water's Way_, a beach scene. "I wanted places for people to say, 'Meet you by the deer'," Smith told _The New York Times_.[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Central_Madison#cite_note-:0-79)

The Madison Concourse level also holds an even larger 120 ft-long (37 m) mosaic by [Yayoi Kusama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yayoi_Kusama "Yayoi Kusama"): _A Message of Love, Directly from My Heart unto the Universe_.[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Central_Madison#cite_note-:0-79)

**Pittsburgh** ([/ˈ p ɪ t s b ɜːr ɡ/](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English")[_PITS-burg_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:Pronunciation_respelling_key "Help:Pronunciation respelling key")) is a city in [Allegheny County, Pennsylvania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania "Allegheny County, Pennsylvania"), United States, and its [county seat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/County_seat "County seat"). Located in [southwestern Pennsylvania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_Pennsylvania "Western Pennsylvania") where the [Allegheny](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Allegheny_River "Allegheny River") and [Monongahela](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monongahela_River "Monongahela River") Rivers meet to form the [Ohio River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ohio_River "Ohio River"), it had a population of 302,971 at the 2020 census, making it the [second-most populous city](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_municipalities_in_Pennsylvania#Municipalities "List of municipalities in Pennsylvania") in Pennsylvania after [Philadelphia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philadelphia "Philadelphia"). The [Pittsburgh metropolitan area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greater_Pittsburgh "Greater Pittsburgh") has over 2.43 million people, making it the largest in the Ohio Valley and [Appalachia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Appalachia "Appalachia"), the [second-largest in Pennsylvania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pennsylvania_metropolitan_areas "Pennsylvania metropolitan areas"), and the [28th-largest in the U.S.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metropolitan_statistical_area#United_States "Metropolitan statistical area") The greater [Pittsburgh–Weirton–Steubenville combined statistical area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsburgh%E2%80%93New_Castle%E2%80%93Weirton_combined_statistical_area "Pittsburgh–New Castle–Weirton combined statistical area") includes parts of [Ohio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ohio "Ohio") and [West Virginia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Virginia "West Virginia").

Pittsburgh is known as "the Steel City" for its dominant role in the [history of the U.S. steel industry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_iron_and_steel_industry_in_the_United_States "History of the iron and steel industry in the United States").[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsburgh#cite_note-Pittsburgh_Names-8) It developed as a vital link of the [Atlantic coast](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mid-Atlantic_(United_States) "Mid-Atlantic (United States)") and [Midwest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Midwestern_United_States#European_exploration_and_early_settlement "Midwestern United States"), as the mineral-rich [Allegheny Mountains](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Allegheny_Mountains "Allegheny Mountains") led to the region being contested by the [French](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_colonial_empire#First_French_colonial_empire "French colonial empire") and [British](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Empire "British Empire") empires, [Virginians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colony_of_Virginia "Colony of Virginia"), [Whiskey Rebels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whiskey_Rebellion "Whiskey Rebellion"), and [Civil War raiders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsburgh_in_the_American_Civil_War "Pittsburgh in the American Civil War").[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsburgh#cite_note-9) For part of the 20th century, Pittsburgh was behind only [New York City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City "New York City") and [Chicago](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago "Chicago") in corporate headquarters employment; it had the most U.S. stockholders per capita.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsburgh#cite_note-10)[Deindustrialization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deindustrialisation_by_country#United_States "Deindustrialisation by country") in the late 20th century resulted in massive layoffs among [blue-collar workers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue-collar_worker "Blue-collar worker") as steel and other heavy industries declined, coinciding with several Pittsburgh-based corporations moving out of the city.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsburgh#cite_note-diaspora-11) However, the city divested from steel and, since the 1990s, Pittsburgh has focused its energies on the healthcare, education, and technology industries.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsburgh#cite_note-12)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsburgh#cite_note-Lubove-1995-13)

Pittsburgh is home to large medical providers, including the [University of Pittsburgh Medical Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Pittsburgh_Medical_Center "University of Pittsburgh Medical Center") and [Allegheny Health Network](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Allegheny_Health_Network "Allegheny Health Network"), as well as [68 colleges and universities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_colleges_and_universities_in_Pittsburgh "List of colleges and universities in Pittsburgh"), including [Carnegie Mellon University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carnegie_Mellon_University "Carnegie Mellon University"), [Duquesne University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duquesne_University "Duquesne University") and the [University of Pittsburgh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Pittsburgh "University of Pittsburgh").[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsburgh#cite_note-edu-14) The area has served as the federal agency headquarters for [cyber defense](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CERT_Coordination_Center "CERT Coordination Center"), [software engineering](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Software_Engineering_Institute "Software Engineering Institute"), [robotics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Robotics_Engineering_Center "National Robotics Engineering Center"), [energy research](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Energy_Technology_Laboratory "National Energy Technology Laboratory"), and the [nuclear navy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bettis_Atomic_Power_Laboratory "Bettis Atomic Power Laboratory").[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsburgh#cite_note-15) The city is home to ten [Fortune 500](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fortune_500 "Fortune 500") companies and seven of the 300 largest U.S. law firms.

Pittsburgh is sometimes called the "City of Bridges" for its [446 bridges](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_bridges_of_Pittsburgh "List of bridges of Pittsburgh").[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsburgh#cite_note-Pittsburgh_Names-8) Its rich industrial history left the area with renowned cultural institutions, including the [Carnegie Museums of Pittsburgh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carnegie_Museums_of_Pittsburgh "Carnegie Museums of Pittsburgh"), [Pittsburgh Zoo & Aquarium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsburgh_Zoo_&_Aquarium "Pittsburgh Zoo & Aquarium"), [Phipps Conservatory and Botanical Gardens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phipps_Conservatory_and_Botanical_Gardens "Phipps Conservatory and Botanical Gardens"), the [National Aviary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Aviary "National Aviary"), and a diverse [cultural district](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cultural_District,_Pittsburgh "Cultural District, Pittsburgh").[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsburgh#cite_note-Ritenbaugh-16) The city's major league [professional sports teams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_in_Pittsburgh "Sports in Pittsburgh") include the [Pittsburgh Steelers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsburgh_Steelers "Pittsburgh Steelers"), [Pittsburgh Penguins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsburgh_Penguins "Pittsburgh Penguins"), and [Pittsburgh Pirates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsburgh_Pirates "Pittsburgh Pirates"). [Jehovah's Witnesses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jehovah's_Witnesses "Jehovah's Witnesses") traces its earliest origins to the city. In 2009, it hosted the [G20 summit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2009_G20_Pittsburgh_summit "2009 G20 Pittsburgh summit").

## Etymology

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Pittsburgh&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Etymology")]

Main article: [Name of Pittsburgh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Name_of_Pittsburgh "Name of Pittsburgh")

Pittsburgh was named in 1758, by Scottish General [John Forbes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Forbes_(British_Army_officer) "John Forbes (British Army officer)"), in honor of British statesman [William Pitt, 1st Earl of Chatham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Pitt,_1st_Earl_of_Chatham "William Pitt, 1st Earl of Chatham"). As Forbes was a [Scotsman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scotsman "Scotsman"), he probably pronounced the name [/ˈ p ɪ t s b ər ə/](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English")[_PITS-bər-ə_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:Pronunciation_respelling_key "Help:Pronunciation respelling key") (similar to [Edinburgh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edinburgh "Edinburgh")).[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsburgh#cite_note-spell-17)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsburgh#cite_note-18)

Pittsburgh was incorporated as a [borough](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Borough_(Pennsylvania) "Borough (Pennsylvania)") on April 22, 1794, with the following Act:[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsburgh#cite_note-19) "Be it enacted by the [Pennsylvania State Senate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pennsylvania_State_Senate "Pennsylvania State Senate") and [Pennsylvania House of Representatives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pennsylvania_House_of_Representatives "Pennsylvania House of Representatives") of the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania ... by the authority of the same, that the said town of Pittsburgh shall be ... erected into a borough, which shall be called the borough of Pittsburgh for ever."[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsburgh#cite_note-20)

From 1891 to 1911, the city's name was federally recognized as "Pittsburg", though use of the final _h_ was retained during this period by the city government and other local organizations.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsburgh#cite_note-21)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsburgh#cite_note-spell-17) After a public campaign, the federal decision to drop the _h_ was reversed.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsburgh#cite_note-spell-17) The _[Pittsburg Press](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsburg\_Press "Pittsburg Press")_ continued spelling the city without an _h_ until 1921.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsburgh#cite_note-22)

### Native Americans

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Pittsburgh&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Native Americans")]

The area of the Ohio headwaters was long inhabited by the [Shawnee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shawnee "Shawnee") and several other settled groups of [Native Americans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indigenous_peoples_of_the_Americas "Indigenous peoples of the Americas").[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsburgh#cite_note-23) The [Seneca people](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seneca_people "Seneca people") called the confluence of the rivers _Diondega_ or _Jaödeogë’_.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsburgh#cite_note-v224-24)[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsburgh#cite_note-Chafe2013-25)[Shannopin's Town](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shannopin's_Town "Shannopin's Town") was an 18th-century [Lenape](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lenape "Lenape") (Delaware) town located roughly from where [Penn Avenue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Penn_Avenue "Penn Avenue") is today, below the mouth of Two Mile Run, from 30th Street to 39th Street. According to [George Croghan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Croghan "George Croghan"), the town was situated on the south bank of the Allegheny, nearly opposite what is now known as Washington's Landing, formerly [Herr's Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herrs_Island,_Pittsburgh "Herrs Island, Pittsburgh"), in what is now the [Lawrenceville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lawrenceville_(Pittsburgh) "Lawrenceville (Pittsburgh)") neighborhood.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsburgh#cite_note-Hanna1-26):289

### 18th century

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Pittsburgh&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: 18th century")]

Further information: [Pennsylvania in the American Revolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pennsylvania_in_the_American_Revolution "Pennsylvania in the American Revolution")

[![Image 26](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/19/Bouquet_blockhouse.JPG/250px-Bouquet_blockhouse.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Bouquet_blockhouse.JPG)

[Fort Pitt Block House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Pitt_Block_House "Fort Pitt Block House"), built by the British in 1764, is the oldest extant structure in Pittsburgh.

The first known European to enter the region was the French explorer [Robert de La Salle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_de_La_Salle "Robert de La Salle") from [Quebec](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quebec "Quebec") during his 1669 expedition down the [Ohio River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ohio_River "Ohio River").[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsburgh#cite_note-27)[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsburgh#cite_note-28) European pioneers, primarily Dutch, followed in the early 18th century. Michael Bezallion was the first to describe the forks of the Ohio in a 1717 manuscript, and later that year European [fur traders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fur_trade "Fur trade") established area posts and settlements.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsburgh#cite_note-chronology-29)

In 1749, French soldiers from Quebec launched an expedition to the forks to unite [Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canada_(New_France) "Canada (New France)") with [French Louisiana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louisiana_(New_France) "Louisiana (New France)") via the rivers.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsburgh#cite_note-chronology-29) During 1753–1754, the British hastily built [Fort Prince George](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Prince_George "Fort Prince George") before a larger French force drove them off. The French built [Fort Duquesne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Duquesne "Fort Duquesne") based on LaSalle's 1669 claims. The [French and Indian War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_and_Indian_War "French and Indian War"), the North American front of the [Seven Years' War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seven_Years'_War "Seven Years' War"), began with the future Pittsburgh as its center. British General [Edward Braddock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Braddock "Edward Braddock") was dispatched with Major [George Washington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Washington "George Washington") as his aide to take Fort Duquesne.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsburgh#cite_note-WDL-30) The British and colonial force were defeated at [Braddock's Field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Braddock's_Field "Braddock's Field"). General John Forbes finally took the forks in 1758. He began construction on [Fort Pitt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Pitt_(Pennsylvania) "Fort Pitt (Pennsylvania)"), named after [William Pitt the Elder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Pitt_the_Elder "William Pitt the Elder"), while the settlement was named "Pittsborough".[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsburgh#cite_note-Lorant-31)

During [Pontiac's War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pontiac's_War "Pontiac's War"), a loose confederation of Native American tribes [laid siege to Fort Pitt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Fort_Pitt "Siege of Fort Pitt") in 1763; the siege was eventually lifted after Colonel [Henry Bouquet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Bouquet "Henry Bouquet") defeated a portion of the besieging force at the [Battle of Bushy Run](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Bushy_Run "Battle of Bushy Run"). Bouquet strengthened the defenses of Fort Pitt the next year.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsburgh#cite_note-EB1911-32)[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsburgh#cite_note-33)[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsburgh#cite_note-34)[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsburgh#cite_note-35)

During this period, the powerful nations of the [Iroquois Confederacy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iroquois_Confederacy "Iroquois Confederacy"), based in New York, had maintained control of much of the Ohio Valley as hunting grounds by right of conquest after defeating other tribes. By the terms of the 1768 [Treaty of Fort Stanwix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Fort_Stanwix "Treaty of Fort Stanwix"), the [Penns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Penn "William Penn") were allowed to purchase the modern region from the [Iroquois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iroquois "Iroquois"). A 1769 survey referenced the future city as the "Manor of Pittsburgh".[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsburgh#cite_note-PCC-36) Both the [Colony of Virginia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colony_of_Virginia "Colony of Virginia") and the [Province of Pennsylvania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Province_of_Pennsylvania "Province of Pennsylvania") claimed the region under their colonial charters until 1780, when they agreed under a federal initiative to extend the [Mason–Dixon line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mason%E2%80%93Dixon_line "Mason–Dixon line") westward, placing Pittsburgh in Pennsylvania. On March 8, 1771, [Bedford County, Pennsylvania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bedford_County,_Pennsylvania "Bedford County, Pennsylvania") was created to govern the frontier.

On April 16, 1771, the city's first civilian local government was created as [Pitt Township](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pitt_Township,_Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania "Pitt Township, Allegheny County, Pennsylvania").[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsburgh#cite_note-37)[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsburgh#cite_note-38) William Teagarden was the first constable, and William Troop was the first clerk.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsburgh#cite_note-39)

Following the [American Revolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Revolution "American Revolution"), the village of Pittsburgh continued to grow. One of its earliest industries was boat building for settlers of the [Ohio Country](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ohio_Country "Ohio Country"). In 1784, Thomas Vickroy completed a town plan which was approved by the Penn family attorney. Pittsburgh became a possession of Pennsylvania in 1785. The following year, the [Pittsburgh Gazette](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsburgh_Post-Gazette "Pittsburgh Post-Gazette") was started, and in 1787, the [Pittsburgh Academy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsburgh_Academy "Pittsburgh Academy") was chartered. Unrest during the [Whiskey Rebellion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whiskey_Rebellion "Whiskey Rebellion") of 1794 resulted in federal troops being sent to the area. By 1797, glass manufacture began, while the population grew to around 1,400. Settlers arrived after crossing the [Appalachian Mountains](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Appalachian_Mountains "Appalachian Mountains") or through the [Great Lakes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Lakes "Great Lakes"). [Fort Pitt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Pitt_(Pennsylvania) "Fort Pitt (Pennsylvania)") (now Pittsburgh) at the source of the Ohio River became the main base for settlers moving into the [Northwest Territory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northwest_Territory "Northwest Territory").

### 19th century

The federal government recognizes Pittsburgh as the starting point for the [Lewis and Clark Expedition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lewis_and_Clark_Expedition "Lewis and Clark Expedition").[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsburgh#cite_note-40) Preparations began in Pittsburgh in 1803 when [Meriwether Lewis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meriwether_Lewis "Meriwether Lewis") purchased a [keelboat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keelboat "Keelboat") that would later be used to ascend the [Missouri River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Missouri_River "Missouri River").[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsburgh#cite_note-41)

The [War of 1812](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_of_1812 "War of 1812") cut off the supply of British goods, stimulating American industry. By 1815, Pittsburgh was producing significant quantities of iron, brass, tin, and glass. On March 18, 1816, the 46-year-old local government became a city. It was served by numerous river steamboats that increased trading traffic on the rivers.

In the 1830s, many [Welsh people](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Welsh_people "Welsh people") from the [Merthyr](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merthyr "Merthyr") steelworks immigrated to the city following the aftermath of the [Merthyr Rising](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merthyr_Rising "Merthyr Rising"). By the 1840s, Pittsburgh was one of the largest cities west of the [Allegheny Mountains](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Allegheny_Mountains "Allegheny Mountains"). The [Great Fire of Pittsburgh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Fire_of_Pittsburgh "Great Fire of Pittsburgh") destroyed over a thousand buildings in 1845. The city rebuilt with the aid of Irish immigrants who came to escape the [Great Famine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Famine_(Ireland) "Great Famine (Ireland)"). By 1857, Pittsburgh's 1,000 factories were consuming 22 million coal bushels yearly. Coal mining and iron manufacturing attracted waves of European immigrants to the area, with the most coming from [Germany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Germany "Germany").

[![Image 29](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/22/Harpers_8_11_1877_Destruction_of_the_Union_Depot.jpg/250px-Harpers_8_11_1877_Destruction_of_the_Union_Depot.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Harpers_8_11_1877_Destruction_of_the_Union_Depot.jpg)

Burning of Union Depot during the [Pittsburgh railroad strike of 1877](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsburgh_railroad_strike_of_1877 "Pittsburgh railroad strike of 1877")

Because Pennsylvania had been established as a free state after the Revolution, enslaved African Americans sought freedom here through escape as refugees from the South, or occasionally fleeing from travelers they were serving who stayed in the city. There were active stations of the [Underground Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underground_Railroad "Underground Railroad") in the city, and numerous refugees were documented as getting help from station agents and African-American workers in city hotels. The Drennen Slave Girl walked out of the Monongahela House in 1850, apparently to freedom.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsburgh#cite_note-freedom-42) The Merchant's Hotel was also a place where African-American workers would advise slaves the state was free and aid them in getting to nearby stations of the Underground Railroad.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsburgh#cite_note-exhibit-43)

Sometimes refugee slaves from the South stayed in Pittsburgh, but other times they continued North, including into Canada. Many slaves left the city and county for Canada after Congress passed the 1850 [Fugitive Slave Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fugitive_Slave_Act "Fugitive Slave Act"), as it required cooperation from law enforcement even in free states and increased penalties. From 1850 to 1860, the black population in Allegheny County dropped from 3,431 to 2,725 as people headed to safety in Canada.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsburgh#cite_note-freedom-42)

The [American Civil War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Civil_War "American Civil War") boosted the city's economy with increased iron and armament demand by the Union. [Andrew Carnegie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Carnegie "Andrew Carnegie") began steel production in 1875 at the [Edgar Thomson Steel Works](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edgar_Thomson_Steel_Works "Edgar Thomson Steel Works") in [North Braddock, Pennsylvania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Braddock,_Pennsylvania "North Braddock, Pennsylvania"), which evolved into the [Carnegie Steel Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carnegie_Steel_Company "Carnegie Steel Company"). He adopted the [Bessemer process](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bessemer_process "Bessemer process") to increase production. Manufacturing was key to the growth of Pittsburgh and the surrounding region. Railroad lines were built into the city along both rivers, increasing transportation access to important markets.

### 20th century

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Pittsburgh&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: 20th century")]

[![Image 30](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e4/Thaddeus_M._Fowler_-_Pittsburgh%2C_Pennsylvania_1902.jpg/250px-Thaddeus_M._Fowler_-_Pittsburgh%2C_Pennsylvania_1902.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Thaddeus_M._Fowler_-_Pittsburgh,_Pennsylvania_1902.jpg)

An aerial view of Pittsburgh in 1902[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsburgh#cite_note-44)

[![Image 31](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f7/Mills_in_Strip_District%2C_Pittsburgh_%2884.41.70%29.jpg/250px-Mills_in_Strip_District%2C_Pittsburgh_%2884.41.70%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Mills_in_Strip_District,_Pittsburgh_(84.41.70).jpg)

Steel mills in the [Strip District](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strip_District,_Pittsburgh "Strip District, Pittsburgh") in 1906

In 1901, [J. P. Morgan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J._P._Morgan "J. P. Morgan") and attorney [Elbert H. Gary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elbert_H._Gary "Elbert H. Gary") merged [Carnegie Steel Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carnegie_Steel_Company "Carnegie Steel Company") and several other companies into [U.S. Steel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Steel "U.S. Steel"). By 1910, Pittsburgh was the [nation's eighth-largest city](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Largest_cities_in_the_United_States_by_population_by_decade "Largest cities in the United States by population by decade"), accounting for between one-third and one-half of national steel output.

The [Pittsburgh Agreement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsburgh_Agreement "Pittsburgh Agreement") was a [memorandum of understanding](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Memorandum_of_understanding "Memorandum of understanding") completed on 31 May 1918 between members of [Czech](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Czechs "Czechs") and [Slovak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slovaks "Slovaks") expatriate communities in the U.S. It replaced the [Cleveland Agreement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cleveland_Agreement "Cleveland Agreement") of 22 October 1915.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsburgh#cite_note-Sabol_Alzo_2009_p._8-45) It concerned the future foundation of [Czechoslovakia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Czechoslovakia "Czechoslovakia") as envisioned by [T. G. Masaryk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/T._G._Masaryk "T. G. Masaryk").[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsburgh#cite_note-46)

The city suffered [severe flooding](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsburgh_flood_of_1936 "Pittsburgh flood of 1936") in March 1936. On March 17 and 18, Pittsburgh sustained its worst flood in history as flood levels rose to a peak of 46 feet. Days of heavy rain and melting snow poured into the city's waterways. At least 62 people died from this tragedy.

The city's population swelled to more than a half million, attracting numerous European immigrants to its industrial jobs. By 1940, non-Hispanic whites were 90.6% of the city's population.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsburgh#cite_note-47) Pittsburgh also became a main destination of the African-American [Great Migration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Migration_(African_American) "Great Migration (African American)") from the rural South during the first half of the 20th century.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsburgh#cite_note-48) Limited initially by discrimination, some 95% percent of the men became unskilled steel workers.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsburgh#cite_note-49)

During [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II"), demand for steel increased and area mills operated 24 hours a day to produce 95 million tons of steel for the war effort.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsburgh#cite_note-Lorant-31) This resulted in the highest levels of air pollution in the city's almost century of industry. The city's reputation as the "arsenal of democracy"[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsburgh#cite_note-50)[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsburgh#cite_note-51) was being overshadowed by [James Parton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Parton "James Parton")'s 1868 observation of Pittsburgh being "hell with the lid off."[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsburgh#cite_note-52)

Following World War II, the city launched a clean air and civic revitalization project known as the "Renaissance," cleaning up the air and the rivers. The "Renaissance II" project followed in 1977, focused on cultural and neighborhood development. The industrial base continued to expand through the 1970s, but beginning in the early 1980s both the area's steel and electronics industries imploded during national industrial restructuring. There were massive layoffs from mill and plant closures.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsburgh#cite_note-diaspora-11)

In the later 20th century, the area shifted its economic base to education, tourism, and services, largely based on healthcare/medicine, finance, and high technology such as robotics. Although Pittsburgh successfully shifted its economy and remained viable, the city's population has never rebounded to its industrial-era highs. While 680,000 people lived in the city proper in 1950, a combination of suburbanization and economic turbulence resulted in a decrease in city population, even as the metropolitan area population increased again.

### 21st century

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Pittsburgh&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: 21st century")]

During the [late 2000s recession](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Late_2000s_recession "Late 2000s recession"), Pittsburgh was economically strong, adding jobs when most cities were losing them. It was one of the few cities in the United States to see housing property values rise. Between 2006 and 2011, the [Pittsburgh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsburgh_metropolitan_area "Pittsburgh metropolitan area")[metropolitan statistical area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metropolitan_statistical_area "Metropolitan statistical area") (MSA) experienced over 10% appreciation in housing prices, the highest appreciation of the largest 25 metropolitan statistical areas in the United States, with 22 of the largest 25 metropolitan statistical areas experiencing depreciations in housing values.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsburgh#cite_note-53)

In September 2009, the [2009 G20 Pittsburgh summit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2009_G20_Pittsburgh_summit "2009 G20 Pittsburgh summit") was held in Pittsburgh.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsburgh#cite_note-54)

In April 2026, Pittsburgh hosted the [NFL](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NFL "NFL") draft for the first time.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsburgh#cite_note-55) The event hosted over 805,000 people in the city during the 3 day event.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsburgh#cite_note-56)

The [Duquesne Incline](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duquesne_Incline "Duquesne Incline") from [Mount Washington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Washington,_Pittsburgh_(mountain) "Mount Washington, Pittsburgh (mountain)")

Pittsburgh has an area of 58.3 square miles (151 km 2), of which 55.6 square miles (144 km 2) is land and 2.8 square miles (7.3 km 2), or 4.75%, is water. The [80th meridian west](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/80th_meridian_west "80th meridian west") passes directly through the city's downtown.

The city is located on the [Allegheny Plateau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Allegheny_Plateau "Allegheny Plateau"), within the [ecoregion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ecoregion "Ecoregion") of the [Western Allegheny Plateau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_Allegheny_Plateau_(ecoregion) "Western Allegheny Plateau (ecoregion)").[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsburgh#cite_note-57) The [Downtown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Downtown_Pittsburgh "Downtown Pittsburgh") area (also known as the Golden Triangle) sits where the [Allegheny River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Allegheny_River "Allegheny River") flows from the northeast and the [Monongahela River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monongahela_River "Monongahela River") from the southeast to form the [Ohio River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ohio_River "Ohio River"). The convergence is at [Point State Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Point_State_Park "Point State Park") and is referred to as "the Point". The city extends east to include the [Oakland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oakland_(Pittsburgh) "Oakland (Pittsburgh)") and [Shadyside](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shadyside_(Pittsburgh) "Shadyside (Pittsburgh)") sections, which are home to the [University of Pittsburgh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Pittsburgh "University of Pittsburgh"), [Carnegie Mellon University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carnegie_Mellon_University "Carnegie Mellon University"), [Chatham University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chatham_University "Chatham University"), [Carnegie Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carnegie_Museums_of_Pittsburgh "Carnegie Museums of Pittsburgh") and [Library](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carnegie_Library_of_Pittsburgh "Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh"), and many other educational, medical, and cultural institutions. The southern, western, and northern areas of the city are primarily residential.

Many [Pittsburgh neighborhoods](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsburgh_neighborhoods "Pittsburgh neighborhoods") are steeply sloped with two-lane roads. More than a quarter of neighborhood names make reference to "hills", "heights", or similar features.[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsburgh#cite_note-58)

The [public stairways in Pittsburgh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_stairways_in_Pittsburgh "Public stairways in Pittsburgh") consist of 800 sets of outdoor public stairways with 44,645 treads and 24,090 vertical feet. They include hundreds of streets composed entirely of stairs, and many other steep streets with stairs for sidewalks.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsburgh#cite_note-59) Many provide vistas of the Pittsburgh area while attracting hikers and fitness walkers.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsburgh#cite_note-60)

Bike and walking trails have been built to border many of the city's rivers and hollows. The [Great Allegheny Passage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Allegheny_Passage "Great Allegheny Passage") and [Chesapeake and Ohio Canal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chesapeake_and_Ohio_Canal "Chesapeake and Ohio Canal") Towpath connect the city directly to downtown Washington, D.C. (some 335 miles [539 km] away) with a continuous bike/running trail.

The city consists of the Downtown area, called the Golden Triangle,[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsburgh#cite_note-61) and four main areas surrounding it: North Side, South Side, East End, and West End. These areas are further divided into 90 neighborhoods.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsburgh#cite_note-62)

[Downtown Pittsburgh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Downtown_Pittsburgh "Downtown Pittsburgh") has 30 skyscrapers, nine over 500 feet (150 m), with the [U.S. Steel Tower](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Steel_Tower "U.S. Steel Tower") being the tallest at 841 ft (256 m).[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsburgh#cite_note-63) The [Cultural District](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cultural_District,_Pittsburgh "Cultural District, Pittsburgh") spans 14 blocks along the Allegheny River and is home to theaters, arts venues, and a growing residential community. The [Firstside](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Firstside_Historic_District "Firstside Historic District") portion of Downtown borders the Monongahela River, the historic Mon Wharf and hosts the distinctive [PPG Place](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PPG_Place "PPG Place") Gothic-style glass skyscraper complex. Downtown is served by the [Port Authority](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Port_Authority_of_Allegheny_County "Port Authority of Allegheny County")'s [light rail system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsburgh_light_rail "Pittsburgh light rail") and [multiple bridges](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bridges_of_Pittsburgh "Bridges of Pittsburgh") leading north and south.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsburgh#cite_note-64) It is also home to [Point Park University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Point_Park_University "Point Park University") and [Duquesne University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duquesne_University "Duquesne University") which borders [Uptown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bluff_(Pittsburgh) "Bluff (Pittsburgh)").

The [North Side](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Side_(Pittsburgh) "North Side (Pittsburgh)"), originally the independent [Allegheny City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Allegheny_City "Allegheny City") until being annexed in 1907, is a primarily residential area with well-preserved 19th-century homes. It hosts attractions like [Acrisure Stadium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Acrisure_Stadium "Acrisure Stadium"), [PNC Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PNC_Park "PNC Park"), the [Andy Warhol Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andy_Warhol_Museum "Andy Warhol Museum"), and the [National Aviary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Aviary "National Aviary"), among others.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsburgh#cite_note-65)

The [South Side](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Side_(Pittsburgh) "South Side (Pittsburgh)"), once home to railyards and mill workers, has seen revitalization with improvements to East Carson Street and new retail. It is now a vibrant neighborhood with diverse shopping and nightlife.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsburgh#cite_note-66) In the 1990s, the [Urban Redevelopment Authority of Pittsburgh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urban_Redevelopment_Authority_of_Pittsburgh "Urban Redevelopment Authority of Pittsburgh") purchased the South Side Works steel mill property and redeveloped it into the [SouthSide Works](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SouthSide_Works "SouthSide Works") mixed-use development.

The East End includes key institutions including the [University of Pittsburgh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Pittsburgh "University of Pittsburgh"), [Carnegie Mellon University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carnegie_Mellon_University "Carnegie Mellon University"), [Carnegie Museums of Art and Natural History](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carnegie_Museums_of_Pittsburgh "Carnegie Museums of Pittsburgh"), and [Phipps Conservatory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phipps_Conservatory "Phipps Conservatory"). It features many parks, including [Mellon Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mellon_Park "Mellon Park"), [Westinghouse Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Westinghouse_Park "Westinghouse Park"), [Schenley Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schenley_Park "Schenley Park"), [Frick Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frick_Park "Frick Park"), [The Frick Pittsburgh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Frick_Pittsburgh "The Frick Pittsburgh"), [Bakery Square](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bakery_Square "Bakery Square"), and the [Pittsburgh Zoo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsburgh_Zoo "Pittsburgh Zoo"), and vibrant neighborhoods like [Shadyside](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shadyside_(Pittsburgh) "Shadyside (Pittsburgh)"). [Squirrel Hill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Squirrel_Hill "Squirrel Hill") is also known as the hub of Jewish life in Pittsburgh, home to approximately 20 synagogues.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsburgh#cite_note-67) Oakland is home to several universities and the [Petersen Events Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Petersen_Events_Center "Petersen Events Center"). The [Strip District](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strip_District,_Pittsburgh "Strip District, Pittsburgh") to the west along the [Allegheny River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Allegheny_River "Allegheny River") is an open-air marketplace by day and a clubbing destination by night. [Bloomfield](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bloomfield_(Pittsburgh) "Bloomfield (Pittsburgh)") is Pittsburgh's Little Italy and is known for its Italian restaurants and grocers. [Lawrenceville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lawrenceville_(Pittsburgh) "Lawrenceville (Pittsburgh)") is a revitalizing rowhouse neighborhood popular with artists and designers. The [Hill District](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hill_District "Hill District") was home to photographer [Charles Harris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Harris_(photographer) "Charles Harris (photographer)") as well as various African-American jazz clubs.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsburgh#cite_note-68)

The [West End](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_End_(Pittsburgh) "West End (Pittsburgh)") includes [Mt. Washington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Washington,_Pittsburgh_(neighborhood) "Mount Washington, Pittsburgh (neighborhood)"), with its famous view of the downtown skyline, and numerous other residential neighborhoods such as [Sheraden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sheraden "Sheraden") and [Elliott](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elliott_(Pittsburgh) "Elliott (Pittsburgh)").

Main article: [Pittsburgh metropolitan area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsburgh_metropolitan_area "Pittsburgh metropolitan area")

[![Image 37: The Puddler, a glass mural of an iron or steel worker in downtown Pittsburgh](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/d/d2/Muralof300SixthStreetBuilding.jpg/250px-Muralof300SixthStreetBuilding.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Muralof300SixthStreetBuilding.jpg)

_The Puddler_, a glass mural of an iron or steel worker,[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsburgh#cite_note-69)[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsburgh#cite_note-70) memorializing Pittsburgh's [industrial heritage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Industrial_heritage "Industrial heritage")

Pennsylvania lies within the Northeastern United States as defined by U.S. Census Bureau regional classifications.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsburgh#cite_note-71)

Pittsburgh lies within the boundaries of [Appalachia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Appalachia "Appalachia") as designated by the [Appalachian Regional Commission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Appalachian_Regional_Commission "Appalachian Regional Commission"), and has long been characterized as a northern urban industrial anchor of Appalachia.[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsburgh#cite_note-72) In its post-industrial era, Pittsburgh has been described as the "Paris of Appalachia",[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsburgh#cite_note-73)[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsburgh#cite_note-74)[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsburgh#cite_note-75)[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsburgh#cite_note-76) in reference to the city's cultural, educational, healthcare, and technological resources. It is the largest city within the Appalachian region.

Geographer Joseph Scarpaci has described Pittsburgh's regional identity as bridging Northeastern and Midwestern influences, characterizing the city as having "one foot in the East... and the other in the Midwest."[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsburgh#cite_note-77)

Pittsburgh is the principal city of the [Pittsburgh Combined Statistical Area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsburgh-New_Castle-Weirton,_PA-OH-WV_Combined_Statistical_Area "Pittsburgh-New Castle-Weirton, PA-OH-WV Combined Statistical Area"), a [combined statistical area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Combined_statistical_area "Combined statistical area") defined by the [U.S. Census Bureau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Census_Bureau "U.S. Census Bureau").
